What you'll learn

  • Create a Colab notebook that lives in your own Google Drive.
  • Run a cell that prints the versions of Python, scikit-learn, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and matplotlib, and stops loudly if scikit-learn is too old.
  • Upgrade scikit-learn inside Colab and restart the session so the upgrade actually loads.
  • Optionally, build the same environment on your own computer with a virtual environment.

Here is a line you will write in Module 2:

On scikit-learn 1.0 that line fails with a TypeError about an unexpected keyword argument, because min_frequency and sparse_output did not exist yet. On a current version it runs fine. This course uses parts of scikit-learn that arrived or changed in recent releases (TargetEncoder, pandas output from transformers, rare-category handling in OneHotEncoder), so the very first thing to settle is which versions you are running. It takes five minutes, and it saves you an afternoon of confusing errors later.

#What you need

  • A Google account. A personal one is the safest choice. Some school accounts have Colab switched off by an administrator, and you'll see a "not allowed" page instead of a notebook.
  • A recent browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari) on any computer, Chromebooks included.
  • Nothing to install. Colab runs your Python on a Google-hosted virtual machine and shows the notebook in your browser. scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib are already there.

A local install is optional and covered further down for people who want to work offline.

#Create your course notebook

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com (opens in a new tab) and sign in with the button at the top right.
  2. Choose File › New notebook in Drive. (If a welcome dialog opens instead, its New notebook button does the same thing.)
  3. Click the name Untitled0.ipynb at the top left and rename it, for example ml-eval-00-setup.ipynb.
  4. Click into the empty code cell, type print("hello from Colab"), and press Shift+Enter.

The first run takes a few seconds while Colab assigns you a machine (a runtime). When it's connected, the top right shows small RAM and Disk bars, and the output appears under the cell. Open Google Drive in another tab: your notebook is in a folder called Colab Notebooks. That folder is where every notebook from this course will live unless you move it.

💡 Tip

Tools › Keyboard shortcuts lists every shortcut. The two you'll use constantly are Shift+Enter (run this cell and move to the next) and Ctrl+Enter (run this cell and stay; Cmd+Enter on a Mac).

#Check your versions

Paste this into a new cell and run it. It prints each library's version and then checks the one this course depends on most.

That output came from the machine that built these pages, so every number and chart in the course comes from scikit-learn 1.8. Your Colab may report a slightly different version. Anything from 1.6 up runs every lesson; small differences in the last decimal place of a score are normal across versions and are not a bug in your code.

The comparison (major, minor) < (1, 6) works because Python compares tuples item by item, so (1, 10) correctly counts as newer than (1, 6). Comparing the version strings directly would get that wrong, since the text "1.10" sorts before "1.6".

#Upgrade scikit-learn when Colab's copy is too old

If the check raised the RuntimeError, run this in a new cell:

Then choose Runtime › Restart session and run the version cell again. The restart is the step people skip. Python had already imported the old scikit-learn into memory, and installing new files on disk does not replace a module that is already loaded. Restarting starts a fresh Python process that imports the new copy.

📝 Note

An upgrade only lasts as long as that runtime. When Colab gives you a fresh machine (after you disconnect, after a long idle period, or the next day), the preinstalled version is back. If you needed the upgrade once, keep the %pip cell at the top of your notebooks.

  2. Open Terminal in a folder for the course and run:

On a Chromebook, Colab is the recommended path. If you have turned on the Linux development environment (or you use a Linux computer), run:

JupyterLab opens in your browser. Create a notebook with File › New › Notebook, pick the Python 3 kernel, and run the same version cell. Each time you come back, activate the environment again before starting jupyter lab.

#Problems you might hit, and the fixes

A page says Colab is not available for your account. Your organization has turned it off. Click your profile picture at the top right of Colab, switch to (or add) a personal Google account, and create the notebook there.

You opened a notebook someone shared, and your edits vanish. Shared notebooks often open in playground mode, which never saves. Choose File › Save a copy in Drive and work in the copy, which belongs to you.

NameError: name 'X' is not defined in a cell that worked an hour ago. The runtime was recycled, so every variable is gone, even though the old outputs are still drawn on the page. Choose Runtime › Run all to rebuild the state from the top.

TypeError: ... got an unexpected keyword argument or ImportError: cannot import name 'TargetEncoder'. Your scikit-learn is older than the lesson's. Run the upgrade cell, restart the session, and check the version again.

Locally: jupyter: command not found or No module named sklearn. The virtual environment isn't active in that terminal. Activate it (the prompt then starts with (.venv)) and try again.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You run %pip install -U scikit-learn, the install succeeds, but sklearn.__version__ still prints the old number. Why?

  • It installed on the same Colab runtime; the files on disk are new.

  • Imported modules stay in memory. Runtime › Restart session starts a fresh process that loads the new files.

  • Colab allows it; the upgrade just isn't loaded yet.

Show answer

B. Imported modules stay in memory. Runtime › Restart session starts a fresh process that loads the new files.

2Why does the version check compare (major, minor) as numbers instead of comparing the strings "1.10" and "1.6"?

  • Text compares character by character, and "1" comes before "6". Integers in a tuple compare correctly.

  • They can; they just compare alphabetically, which is wrong for version numbers.

  • Some do (like 1.8.dev0), but the real issue is the alphabetical ordering.

Show answer

A. Text compares character by character, and "1" comes before "6". Integers in a tuple compare correctly.

Key takeaways

  • Colab needs only a Google account and a browser, and saves notebooks to Colab Notebooks in your Drive.
  • Print your library versions at the top of every project notebook; this course needs scikit-learn 1.6 or newer.
  • After %pip install -U, restart the session, or the old version stays loaded.
  • A recycled runtime keeps the old outputs on screen but loses every variable: Runtime › Run all rebuilds them.

  • Installing scikit-learn (opens in a new tab): the official instructions for every operating system, including virtual environments.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Name the places where randomness enters a scikit-learn workflow.
  • Make a cross-validated score identical on every run with random_state.
  • Explain why random_state=0 and random_state=np.random.RandomState(0) give different results when a splitter is reused.
  • Measure how far a score moves when only the seed changes, and use that as a yardstick for "real" differences.
  • Run a smoke test that exercises every library the course uses.

Run this cell three times in a row, or just read the output: the loop already does it three times.

Same data, same model, same code, and three different answers. If you were comparing this forest with another model, which of the three numbers would go in your report? None of them should, until you control where the randomness comes from. This course is about comparisons you can defend, and a comparison you can't repeat isn't one.

#Where randomness hides

A typical workflow has several independent sources of randomness, and each one needs its own seed:

In the cell above, two of them were left free: KFold(shuffle=True) reshuffled which patients landed in which fold, and the forest drew different bootstrap samples and feature subsets for its trees. Models that don't use randomness (plain linear regression, k-nearest neighbors) have no random_state parameter at all, which is a quick way to tell.

#Pin it with random_state

Give every random component an integer seed, and the three runs collapse into one number:

Keep one SEED constant at the top of the notebook and pass it everywhere. Changing a single line then reruns the whole analysis under a new seed, which you'll do in a moment on purpose.

For random numbers you generate yourself (synthetic data, noise, a random subset of rows), use NumPy's Generator: rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED). Keep it separate from scikit-learn's random_state, which accepts None, an integer, or a legacy np.random.RandomState object, but not a Generator.

#An integer seed and a RandomState object are not the same

Here's a subtle one that bites careful people. You might think passing a seeded RandomState object is the same as passing the integer. Watch what happens when the same splitter is used twice:

With an integer, the splitter restarts from the same seed on every call to split, so every model you evaluate with cv_int sees identical folds. With a RandomState object, each call draws from the object's stream and moves it forward, so the second call produces different folds. Compare two models with cv_obj and you have compared them on different test sets, which muddies exactly the difference you were trying to measure.

⚠️ Watch out

Pass integers to splitters and models when you compare things. A shared RandomState object (or random_state=None) gives each model different folds, so part of the gap between two scores is just the folds changing.

#A seed is not a result

Pinning a seed makes a number repeatable. It doesn't make it right: seed 0 is just one draw out of many equally valid ones. So measure how much the score moves when you change only the seed. Here the forest seed and the fold seed are varied separately, ten values each:

Look at the printed ranges. On this dataset, reshuffling the folds moves the score about three times as much as reseeding the forest. Now suppose a second model beats this one by 0.02 under seed 0. That gap is smaller than the spread you get from reshuffling alone, so it tells you nothing yet. Module 3 turns this into a proper tool (repeated cross-validation and fold-by-fold comparisons), but the habit starts here: before you believe a difference, know how big the noise is.

📝 Note

The same seed can still give slightly different numbers on a different machine. Library versions, the math library NumPy was built with, and multithreaded code can change the last few digits. That's why the setup lesson had you print versions: when two people's results disagree in the third decimal place, versions are the first thing to compare.

#Smoke test: one cell that touches everything

The last step proves the toolkit works end to end: a pandas DataFrame with a text column, a ColumnTransformer, a Pipeline, cross_validate with two metrics, and an assertion that fails loudly if anything is off. Paste it into your setup notebook and keep it there.

If this prints Smoke test passed, every library is installed, they work together, and your numbers match the page. The assert line is a cheap habit worth keeping: it turns "this looks about right" into a check that stops the notebook when something drifts. Notice also the neg_ in the scorer name. scikit-learn always maximizes scores, so error metrics come back negated, and you flip the sign to report them.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You compare a forest and a boosted model with cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=np.random.RandomState(1)), calling cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv) for each. What's wrong?

  • The object is seeded once, but each split call advances it, so the second model gets different folds.

  • Use random_state=1 (an integer) so every call to split produces the same folds.

  • It does accept one; it just behaves differently from an integer.

Show answer

B. Use random_state=1 (an integer) so every call to split produces the same folds.

2Under seed 0, model B beats model A by 0.01 R^2. Reshuffling the folds alone moves A's score by about 0.07. What should you conclude?

  • A positive gap smaller than the seed-to-seed noise could easily flip under another seed.

  • You need repeated or paired comparisons (Module 3) before calling a winner.

  • Seed 0 is no worse than any other seed; it's just one draw.

Show answer

B. You need repeated or paired comparisons (Module 3) before calling a winner.

3Which of these models has no random_state parameter because it never draws random numbers?

  • Forests bootstrap rows and sample features, so they need a seed.

  • Least squares has one exact solution, so the same data always gives the same model.

  • Shuffling is random, so the splitter takes a random_state.

Show answer

B. Least squares has one exact solution, so the same data always gives the same model.

Key takeaways

  • Randomness enters through data generation, splitting, fold shuffling, model internals, and search sampling; seed each one.
  • Keep one SEED constant and pass it as an integer; a shared RandomState object gives each call different folds.
  • Use np.random.default_rng(SEED) for random numbers you generate yourself.
  • A pinned seed is repeatable, not representative. Measure the seed-to-seed spread before trusting a small difference.
  • Keep a smoke-test cell with an assert at the top of your setup notebook.

#Further reading

  • Controlling randomness (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's own guide to integers versus RandomState instances, with recommendations for estimators and splitters.
  • NumPy random Generator (opens in a new tab): how default_rng works and why it replaced the old np.random.seed style.
  • Glossary: random_state (opens in a new tab): the precise definition of what each kind of value does.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a notebook must survive Restart session and run all, and spot the hidden-state bug that breaks it.
  • Lay out a project notebook in the section order this course uses.
  • Record each experiment (model, validation scheme, mean and spread of the score) in a CSV log you can sort later.
  • Save notebooks and output files somewhere that outlives a Colab runtime.
  • Fix the three scikit-learn errors you'll see most often.

Notebooks let you run cells in any order, and that freedom is how most notebook bugs are born. Here is a tiny table of patients and a cell that removes the age column:

That worked. Now imagine you tweak something below, scroll back up, and run the same cell again:

The code didn't change; the state did. The first run already removed age, so the second run has nothing to drop. The reverse problem is sneakier: a notebook that only works because you once ran a cell you've since deleted. Both bugs disappear under one test.

#The one test every notebook must pass

Before you trust a result or share a notebook, choose Runtime › Restart session and run all in Colab (in JupyterLab, Kernel › Restart Kernel and Run All Cells). That throws away every variable and runs the cells top to bottom, exactly as someone else would. If it finishes without errors and prints the same numbers, the notebook is reproducible. If it doesn't, you've just found a bug before your reader did.

Two rules make the test easy to pass. Never let a cell modify a variable it also reads, as the drop cell did; write features = patients.drop(columns="age") instead, so rerunning it is harmless. And put every import and constant in the first cell, so no later cell depends on something you typed once and forgot.

#A template for every project in this course

Every Build-along and the capstone follow the same section order. The order matters more than the headings: data flows down the page, and the test set is touched exactly once, near the end.

The loop from Log back to Pipeline is where you'll spend most of your time: change one thing, validate, log, repeat. The arrow to Final test is taken once. Use text cells (+ Text in Colab) for the numbered headings, so the table of contents in Colab's left sidebar becomes a map of your project.

#Keep an experiment log

Two weeks into a project, nobody remembers whether the 0.47 came from five folds or ten, or which preprocessing it used. A log fixes that. This function appends one row per experiment to a CSV file, including the spread of the fold scores, not just the mean:

Now run two quick experiments on the diabetes data and log both:

pd.read_csv(LOG) turns the log back into a DataFrame, so later you can sort by mean, filter by cv, or plot every experiment you ever ran. Rerunning a cell adds rows rather than replacing them. That's deliberate: the log is a history, and a rerun with a different result is worth knowing about.

#Save work somewhere that survives

Colab saves the notebook to Drive automatically, and File › Revision history lets you roll back. Files your code writes, like experiments.csv, are different: they live on the runtime's disk under /content, and they're deleted when the runtime is recycled. To keep them, mount your Drive and write there:

That block only works inside Colab, which is why it isn't run on this page. For extra copies, File › Download › Download .ipynb saves the notebook to your computer, and File › Save a copy in GitHub pushes it to a repository you own.

#Read scikit-learn errors from the bottom up

A traceback can run to thirty lines, but the useful part is almost always the last line (what went wrong) and the last line that mentions your own file (where). Here are the three errors you'll meet most, each produced on purpose.

Text where a number should be.

Models only accept numbers, and the message even quotes the offending value. The fix is to encode the column, with OneHotEncoder inside a ColumnTransformer, which is Module 2's first topic.

A blank cell.

Read the full message under the traceback: scikit-learn names the estimator that rejected the NaN and suggests the two usual fixes, imputing (a SimpleImputer in the pipeline) or switching to a model that handles missing values natively, like HistGradientBoostingClassifier.

Using a step before fitting it.

transform applies what fit learned, and a fresh scaler hasn't learned anything. In practice this usually means you built a new object instead of reusing the fitted one, or you called fit on a copy.

💡 Tip

When an error makes no sense, check two things before anything else: X.dtypes (is a "number" column secretly text?) and X.shape (did a step drop rows or columns you expected to keep?). Those two lines explain a surprising share of confusing failures.

#When you're stuck for more than ten minutes

  1. Restart and run all. A surprising number of bugs are stale state.
  2. Read the last line of the traceback, then find the last line that mentions your code.
  3. Shrink the problem. Copy the failing part into a new cell with five rows of made-up data. If the error survives, you have a minimal reproducer; if it vanishes, the difference between the two versions is your clue.
  4. Search the exact message in quotes, without your variable names, and check the scikit-learn page for the function you called.
  5. Ask with the reproducer, your versions from section 0, and what you expected to happen. Someone can answer that in a minute; "my model doesn't work" can't be answered at all.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Which of these cells gives the same result no matter how many times you run it?

  • Each run divides again, so after three runs every income is a billion times too small, and nothing warns you.

  • The second run raises KeyError, because the first run already removed the column.

  • It reads df and writes a different name, so df never changes and every rerun computes the same adults.

Show answer

C. It reads df and writes a different name, so df never changes and every rerun computes the same adults.

2Your experiment log in /content/experiments.csv is gone the next morning, but the notebook is fine. Why?

  • It deletes the whole runtime disk, not CSV files in particular.

  • Mount Drive and write the log to a path under /content/drive/MyDrive.

  • The with block closes the file and writes it to disk immediately.

Show answer

B. Mount Drive and write the log to a path under /content/drive/MyDrive.

Key takeaways

  • Restart session and run all is the test of a reproducible notebook; cells that overwrite their own inputs fail it.
  • Follow the template: setup, data, split, pipeline, validate, log, final test once, notes.
  • Log every experiment with its validation scheme and the std of the fold scores, not just the mean.
  • Notebooks save to Drive; files under /content don't. Mount Drive for anything you want to keep.
  • Read tracebacks from the bottom; check X.dtypes and X.shape first.

#Further reading

  • Crafting a minimal reproducer for scikit-learn (opens in a new tab): the maintainers' guide to shrinking a bug report until it's answerable.
  • External data: local files, Drive, Sheets, and Cloud Storage (opens in a new tab): Colab's official notebook on reading and writing files, including mounting Drive.
  • scikit-learn FAQ (opens in a new tab): answers to the questions people ask most, from missing values to string features.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what fit stores and what transform reuses, and why that keeps training and prediction consistent.
  • Build a ColumnTransformer that imputes, scales, and one-hot encodes a mixed-type DataFrame, including categories it has never seen.
  • Turn hand-written feature code into pipeline steps with FunctionTransformer and a custom transformer class.
  • Show, with numbers, how preprocessing that learns from labels leaks when it runs outside cross-validation.

A churn model for a video-streaming service was trained in a notebook with a cell like this, run once on the whole table. It contains a bug that takes months to show up:

Months later, the app team sends five new customers to score. The model expects a tenure_days column that the raw rows don't have, so someone copies the cell into the scoring script. Now the missing ages are filled with the median of those five customers, a number that has nothing to do with the one the model was trained on. Nothing crashes. The predictions are just quietly wrong.

The fix is to make feature engineering part of the model object, so that one fit learns everything from training rows and one predict replays it on any rows you hand it. Every lesson in this module uses a synthetic version of that streaming service's data, so we know the true rules behind it:

Read the logit line once: churn depends on viewing hours per device, support tickets, plan, payment type, tenure, and age. Postcode has no effect at all. Remember that; it will matter at the end.

#fit learns, transform replays

Every scikit-learn preprocessor follows one contract. fit looks at training data and stores what it learned in attributes whose names end in an underscore. transform uses those stored values and learns nothing new. Step through a stripped-down imputer written in plain Python and watch where median_ comes from:

Both batches get 41, the training median, whatever else is in the batch. That is the property the streaming team's notebook lost. Suppose the five new customers came from a campus promotion; here is how far apart the two fill values end up:

#Route each column to its own steps

Numbers need imputing and scaling; text categories need encoding; some columns shouldn't reach the model at all. ColumnTransformer sends each group of columns through its own steps and glues the results side by side:

Three details in that output are worth knowing:

  • add_indicator=True appended missingindicator_watch_hours and missingindicator_age, flags that record that a value was blank. (They start as 0/1; the scaler then rescales them like every other numeric column, which is why they print as -0.23 and -0.29.) When blanks aren't random, say people who hide their age behave differently, the flag carries signal that the median alone erases.
  • min_frequency=30 merged crypto (25 training rows) into payment_infrequent_sklearn. A category with a handful of rows gives the model a coefficient it can't estimate well.
  • handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist" sends categories never seen in training into that same infrequent column instead of crashing.

set_output(transform="pandas") makes the transformer return a DataFrame with readable names, which makes debugging much easier than staring at a bare array.

#Write features as steps, not cells

Feature code that doesn't learn anything (dates to durations, ratios, logs) becomes a step with FunctionTransformer. Code that needs parameters, or that should report its output column names, is cleaner as a small class. The rules for a scikit-learn-compatible class are short: __init__ only stores its arguments under the same names, fit returns self (and stores anything learned with a trailing underscore), and transform returns the new data.

Inheriting from BaseEstimator gives you get_params and set_params for free, which is what lets clone, cross-validation, and grid search copy your step and change its snapshot. That only works if __init__ stores arguments unchanged. Converting snapshot to a Timestamp inside __init__ looks harmless but breaks under a search: GridSearchCV changes settings with set_params, which assigns attributes directly and never runs __init__, so searched values would arrive as raw strings. Do conversions in fit or transform.

#When preprocessing learns from labels, leaking gets loud

Fitting a scaler on all rows leaks a little: test rows nudge the mean. Preprocessing that uses the target leaks a lot. Target encoding replaces each category with the average outcome for that category, which is a tempting way to handle a column like postcode with 300 levels. Done with pandas before cross-validation, each row's encoding includes its own label. Done with TargetEncoder inside the pipeline, each training row is encoded from the other folds (scikit-learn calls this cross fitting), and validation rows only see rates learned from training rows.

The leaky version looks like a real improvement on every fold, and it is pure fiction: we built the data, and postcode does nothing. With roughly four customers per postcode, a row's own label is a quarter of its "postcode rate", so the feature partly is the answer. Inside the pipeline, the encoder adds nothing, which is the truth. A score that jumps when you add a high-cardinality column deserves suspicion before celebration.

#Mistakes that slip past code review

⚠️ Watch out

Unknown categories crash the default encoder. OneHotEncoder() uses handle_unknown="error", so the first customer who pays with a method training never saw takes down your scoring job. Pick "ignore" (all zeros) or "infrequent_if_exist" (the rare bucket) on purpose.

⚠️ Watch out

remainder="drop" is the default. Any column you forget to list silently disappears, and the model trains without it. List every column deliberately, or set remainder="passthrough" while exploring, and print get_feature_names_out() to see what actually reaches the model.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A pipeline's SimpleImputer(strategy="median") was fit on training data where the median age was 44. You call predict on a batch of new customers whose median age is 29. What value fills their missing ages?

  • transform replays statistics_ learned at fit time; the new batch's own median is never computed.

  • That's what the hand-written notebook cell did, and it's the inconsistency pipelines prevent.

  • The fill value is fixed after fit, whatever the batch looks like.

Show answer

A. transform replays statistics_ learned at fit time; the new batch's own median is never computed.

2A custom transformer's __init__ does self.snapshot = pd.Timestamp(snapshot), and transform subtracts dates from self.snapshot. What happens when a grid search tries snapshot values ["2025-07-01", "2025-10-01"]?

  • It would, if the search built each candidate by calling __init__; it doesn't.

  • scikit-learn assigns searched values straight to attributes. Keep __init__ to plain storage and convert inside fit or transform.

  • The order of calls doesn't change; the problem is where the conversion lives.

Show answer

B. scikit-learn assigns searched values straight to attributes. Keep __init__ to plain storage and convert inside fit or transform.

3Adding a target-encoded postcode raises cross-validated AUC from 0.80 to 0.89, but the encoding was computed with groupby(...).transform("mean") on all training rows. What should you do first?

  • The jump is what leakage looks like; you can't tell it apart from real signal yet.

  • If the gain survives cross fitting, it's real. Here it vanishes.

  • More folds give a more precise estimate of a leaky number.

Show answer

B. If the gain survives cross fitting, it's real. Here it vanishes.

4Which column is the best candidate for min_frequency grouping?

  • min_frequency is a one-hot encoder setting for categories, not numbers.

  • A level with a few dozen rows gets a poorly estimated coefficient; grouping it is safer.

  • Every level has hundreds of rows, so there's nothing rare to group.

Show answer

B. A level with a few dozen rows gets a poorly estimated coefficient; grouping it is safer.

Key takeaways

  • fit stores what it learns in attributes ending in _; transform replays them, so new rows are treated exactly like training rows.
  • A ColumnTransformer routes each column group to its own steps; list columns deliberately, because unlisted ones are dropped.
  • Set handle_unknown on purpose, and use min_frequency to merge rare levels.
  • Feature code belongs in FunctionTransformer steps or small BaseEstimator classes whose __init__ stores arguments unchanged.
  • Anything that learns from labels, like target encoding, must be fitted inside cross-validation; outside it, a useless column can look like a breakthrough.

#Further reading

  • Pipelines and composite estimators (opens in a new tab): the user guide for Pipeline, ColumnTransformer, FunctionTransformer, and parameter names inside nested steps.
  • Target Encoder's internal cross fitting (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's own demonstration of why fit_transform and fit().transform() differ for this encoder.
  • Developing scikit-learn estimators (opens in a new tab): the full rules for writing your own transformer, including why __init__ must not validate or convert.

  • Use plots and tables of the training data to decide which features to build.
  • Score rows straight from an app, with blanks and unseen categories, without any manual preparation.
  • Package the model so another program can load it.

The model you'll finish with takes a raw customer record, exactly as the app stores it, and returns a churn probability. Every arrow below is a pipeline step, so a single fit learns all of them from training rows:

Each step below adds one piece and re-runs the same 5-fold cross-validation on the training set, so you can see what every feature is worth. The test set stays locked until Step 6.

#Step 1: Data, split, and a raw-column baseline

The generator is the same one from the Notes lesson. Run it, split once, and score a pipeline that uses only the columns as they arrive.

That's the number every feature has to beat. columns_step takes the list of numeric columns as an argument, because the list grows as we engineer features; building the transformer from a function means each version is a fresh object.

#Step 2: Turn dates and ratios into features

Two features need no learning at all. A signup date means nothing to a linear model, but days since signup does. And raw viewing hours mix up two things: a family sharing five screens at 40 hours is less engaged than one person at 40 hours, so we divide by devices and take a log to tame the long right tail.

A big jump from two lines of pandas. Because add_features sits inside the pipeline, it runs on validation folds, the test set, and next month's customers in exactly the same way. Note out = frame.copy(): a step that edits its input in place would change X_train itself the first time it runs.

#Step 3: Let the training data suggest features

Good features usually come from looking. Here are churn rates by age band and by a pair of conditions, computed on training rows only, so this exploration can't leak test information into our choices:

Two findings. Churn is high at both ends of the age range, but logistic regression gives age one coefficient, so it can only say "older means more" or "older means less". A feature measuring distance from the typical age lets a straight line describe a U. And customers in their first year who filed two or more tickets churn far more than either condition alone would suggest; that's an interaction, which a linear model also can't build by itself.

The interaction is a fixed rule, so it joins add_features. The age distance needs a center, and the center should be learned from training rows, so it gets a small class with a real fit:

During cross-validation, DistanceFromTypical is cloned and refit inside each fold, so every fold computes its center from its own training part. Missing ages stay missing in age_gap, and the imputer downstream handles both columns.

#Step 4: Read what the model learned

Fit on the full training set and line up each output column with its coefficient. Inputs were scaled, so coefficients are roughly comparable in size.

Because we generated this data, we can check the model against the truth: more viewing per device and longer tenure lower risk, gift cards and tickets raise it, and age matters through its gap from typical. Postcode never reached the model, which is right, since it carries no signal.

#Step 5: Score rows straight from the app

Here are three new customers as the app would send them, with a blank age, a payment method the training data never contained, and a postcode nobody in training had.

No preparation code, no crash. The blank age was filled with the training median, apple_pay landed in the infrequent bucket, and the unknown postcode was dropped with the rest of the unlisted columns. The first customer, a three-month-old basic account that has already filed two support tickets, is flagged as high risk; that is the first-year interaction at work. The 71-year-old gets a moderate score mostly through age_gap.

#Step 6: Open the test set once

Every choice so far was made with cross-validation on training rows. Now, and only now, score the 375 customers we set aside:

The test score lands close to the cross-validated one, which is what you hope for when nothing leaked. If the test score had come out much higher than CV, that would be worth investigating too: it usually means a lucky split or a leak, not a better model.

#The finished program

In a real project the feature code lives in its own .py file, because a saved model only stores a reference to your custom class and function. When another program loads the model, Python must be able to import them by the same names, or loading fails with an AttributeError about a missing attribute on __main__. This script is laid out that way: run it with python churn_pipeline.py, or split the top half into churn_features.py and import from it.

⚠️ Watch out

Only load .joblib or pickle files you created or fully trust. Loading one runs code chosen by whoever saved it, so a model file from a stranger is as risky as a script from a stranger.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is the typical age learned in DistanceFromTypical.fit instead of hard-coded as 45 inside add_features?

  • It would run fine; the problem is where the number comes from.

  • A value picked by looking at all the data is a small leak; learning it in fit keeps every fold honest.

  • add_features already uses the constant SNAPSHOT; constants are fine when they don't come from the data.

Show answer

B. A value picked by looking at all the data is a small leak; learning it in fit keeps every fold honest.

2The age-band chart and crosstab were computed on X_train only. What would go wrong if you used the full df?

  • Looking is a form of fitting. Decisions made after seeing test labels leak into the test score.

  • A human choosing features from the chart is part of the training process.

  • pd.cut puts blank ages in no band; the chart would still draw.

Show answer

A. Looking is a form of fitting. Decisions made after seeing test labels leak into the test score.

3A colleague loads churn_model.joblib in a scoring service and gets AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'add_features' on <module '__main__'>. What's the fix?

  • The protocol isn't the issue; the file references a class the service can't find.

  • The saved file stores the class's module and name. If those don't resolve in the loading program, it fails.

  • Lambdas can't be pickled by name at all, which makes the problem worse.

Show answer

B. The saved file stores the class's module and name. If those don't resolve in the loading program, it fails.

Key takeaways

  • Measure a raw baseline first; every engineered feature then has a number to beat.
  • Rules that need no data (dates to durations, ratios, interactions) go in a FunctionTransformer; anything learned from data goes in a class with a real fit.
  • Explore on training rows only, because choosing features is part of fitting.
  • A pipeline scores raw rows with blanks and unseen categories without extra code.
  • Keep custom steps in an importable module so a saved model can be loaded elsewhere, and only load model files you trust.

What you'll learn

  • Predict exactly which columns come out of a ColumnTransformer.
  • Choose between handle_unknown="ignore" and "infrequent_if_exist" for a given situation.
  • Write a FunctionTransformer and a stateful custom transformer that follow scikit-learn's rules.
  • Find a leak that comes from imputation, and measure how much it inflates a score.
  • Use TransformedTargetRegressor to model a skewed target.

Run this setup cell first. Every exercise builds its own small data, so you can do them in any order after it.

#Warm-up: count the output columns

Without running anything: a ColumnTransformer sends ["age", "income"] through StandardScaler and ["city"] (four distinct cities in training) through OneHotEncoder(). The input has five columns. How many columns come out?

Show solution

Six. Two scaled numbers plus four one-hot columns. The fifth input column isn't listed, and the default remainder="drop" throws it away. If that surprised you, Exercise 1 is for you.

#Exercise 1: The column that vanished

A teammate's model ignores days_since_login, one of the strongest churn signals, and they can't see why. Print the output feature names of their transformer, explain the problem, then fix it two ways: by listing the column, and by using remainder.

Sample output after your fix:

Need a hint?

Call teammate.fit(logins) and then get_feature_names_out(). For the remainder fix, think about what else would pass through, and whether you want it to.

Show solution

Unlisted columns are dropped by default, so days_since_login never reached the model. Listing it is the better fix. remainder="passthrough" also lets through user_id, an identifier the model should never see (and a text column that would crash LogisticRegression). It also leaves days_since_login unscaled. Passthrough is useful while exploring; in a final pipeline, list every column you mean to use.

#Exercise 2: New and rare categories

A device-type column has 40 phone rows, 30 tv, 3 console, and 2 car in training. Fit two encoders: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=5). Before running, predict the output for the rows ["console", "watch"] from each. Then decide which you'd use for a churn model, and why.

Need a hint?

With min_frequency=5, any category seen fewer than 5 times during fit joins one shared infrequent column. With "ignore", an unseen category becomes a row of zeros.

Show solution

With "ignore", console keeps its own column (learned from 3 rows) and watch becomes all zeros, which the model reads as "none of the known devices". With the infrequent setting, console and car share one column, and the unseen watch lands there too. For churn, the second is usually better: three rows can't support a reliable coefficient, and "a rare device" is a sensible guess for a device you've never seen.

#Exercise 3: Put the clock on a circle

Login hour runs from 0 to 23. As a plain number, 23:00 and 00:00 look 23 units apart even though they're one hour apart. Write a FunctionTransformer that replaces hour with hour_sin and hour_cos (angle = 2π·hour/24). Check that the distance between 23 and 0 is now smaller than between 23 and 12, and plot the 24 encoded points.

Need a hint?

np.sin(2 * np.pi * hour / 24) and the same with np.cos. Return a DataFrame from your function so the column names survive, and pass feature_names_out a function that returns the new names if you want get_feature_names_out() to work.

Show solution

A model now sees 23:00 and 00:00 as neighbours. You need both sine and cosine: sine alone gives 03:00 and 09:00 the same value. This transformer learns nothing, so FunctionTransformer is the right tool.

#Exercise 4: A transformer that learns its limits

Write QuantileClipper(lower=0.01, upper=0.99). fit stores each column's lower and upper quantile from the training data in bounds_; transform clips values to those bounds. It must work inside a pipeline (inherit from the right classes, keep __init__ simple), and calling transform before fit should raise scikit-learn's NotFittedError. Test it on a column with one huge outlier, then transform a new batch and confirm it uses the training bounds.

Need a hint?

X.quantile([self.lower, self.upper]) on a DataFrame gives both bounds for every column at once. DataFrame.clip(lower=..., upper=..., axis=1) clips each column to its own bounds. from sklearn.utils.validation import check_is_fitted and call check_is_fitted(self) at the top of transform.

Show solution

check_is_fitted looks for attributes ending in _, which is one more reason to follow the naming rule. The new batch's 9999 is clipped to the training upper bound, so the outlier in tomorrow's data can't shift the limits.

#Exercise 5: The imputer that peeked

A lab-results dataset has its two most useful measurements missing in about half the rows. Someone fills the blanks with KNNImputer on a table that still includes the outcome column, then cross-validates. Run their code, then write the honest version with the imputer inside the pipeline and without the outcome. How big is the gap, and why does it happen?

Need a hint?

KNNImputer fills a blank by averaging the nearest rows. Ask yourself which column makes two rows look "near" when the outcome is part of the distance.

Show solution

With the outcome in the table, each blank is filled from neighbours that mostly share the row's own label, so the filled-in values quietly encode the answer. Two mistakes stack: the label was an imputation input, and the imputer saw validation rows. At prediction time there is no label to use, so the leaky score can never be reached in practice. Inside the pipeline, the imputer only sees features, and only from each fold's training part.

#Exercise 6: A skewed target

Monthly spend is positive and right-skewed: most customers spend $10–$35, and a few spend over $100. Compare a scaled Ridge fitted on raw spend with the same model wrapped in TransformedTargetRegressor(func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1). Report mean and median absolute error from 5-fold CV. Which errors improve more, and why?

Need a hint?

from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor. Pass scoring=["neg_mean_absolute_error", "neg_median_absolute_error"] to cross_validate and flip the signs.

Show solution

Spend grows multiplicatively with visits and plan here, so a straight line fits the log of spend far better than spend itself. The median error, which describes the typical customer, improves most; the raw model was bending itself toward the few huge spenders. The wrapper also handles the round trip: you call predict and get dollars back, and cross-validation scores in dollars too.

#Challenge: a pipeline that adapts to any table

Write a preprocessing transformer that works on any DataFrame without listing column names: numbers get median imputation and scaling, text columns get one-hot encoding with an infrequent bucket. Add a custom MissingCount step that appends one column, n_missing, counting blanks per row, and give it a get_feature_names_out so .set_output(transform="pandas") works. Run it unchanged on two tables: the logins frame from Exercise 1 (with a blank added) and X_spend from Exercise 6.

Need a hint?

from sklearn.compose import make_column_selector and use make_column_selector(dtype_include="number") and make_column_selector(dtype_include=object) in place of column lists. Put MissingCount before the ColumnTransformer so it counts the original blanks, and let the numeric selector pick up n_missing automatically. get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None) should return the input names plus "n_missing"; store the input names in fit as self.feature_names_in_ = np.asarray(X.columns).

Show solution

The selectors are evaluated at fit time, so the same recipe adapts to each table's columns. (In the four-row table, premium and standard appear once each, so min_frequency=2 merges them into the infrequent column; with real data you'd pick a larger threshold.) Notice that n_missing is created before the column selection, so the numeric selector picks it up and scales it like any other number. Selecting by dtype has one risk: an ID stored as text gets one-hot encoded, so drop identifiers before the pipeline, as done with user_id here.

What you'll learn

  • Show how a single train/test split can reverse a model comparison.
  • Explain how KFold assigns rows to folds, and when to shuffle.
  • Choose between KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, and TimeSeriesSplit from the structure of a dataset.
  • Report several metrics at once with cross_validate, including their spread across folds.
  • Explain why the best score from a search is optimistic, and how nested cross-validation fixes it.

Two models, one 300-row dataset, forty different random 75/25 splits. Here's how often each model "wins":

A test set of 75 rows is small, so which 75 rows you get moves accuracy by almost twenty points, and the "better" model changes with the seed. The fix isn't a bigger single test set (you rarely have spare data). It's to use every row for testing exactly once and look at the whole distribution of scores, which is what cross-validation does. The harder question, and the subject of this lesson, is how to carve the data so each test fold is a fair stand-in for the future.

#How KFold carves up the rows

With n_splits=k, KFold cuts the rows into k blocks of nearly equal size, uses each block once as the test fold, and trains on the rest. When the rows don't divide evenly, the first few folds get one extra row. Step through the sizing for 7 rows and 3 folds:

Without shuffle=True, the blocks are consecutive rows. That's fine if the rows are in random order and a disaster if they're sorted (by class, by date, by hospital), because a test fold can then contain kinds of rows the training folds never saw. Shuffle by default, with an integer random_state, unless order carries meaning, which is the time-series case below.

#Four splitters, four assumptions

Each splitter encodes a belief about how your data relates to the future data the model will meet. Here's how each one assigns 24 rows across four splits. The data has a rare class (triangles), and the rows come in groups of three, like three visits per patient (the gray stripes).

StratifiedKFold keeps each class's share the same in every fold. With a rare class that matters a lot. Here 11 positives out of 150 rows go through plain shuffled KFold and through StratifiedKFold:

One KFold test fold has no positives at all, so recall and ROC AUC can't even be computed on it, while another has five. Stratifying removes that source of noise for free. (When you pass an integer for cv to a classifier, scikit-learn already uses stratified folds; pass a splitter object when you want shuffling and a seed.)

GroupKFold keeps every row of a group in the same fold. Use it whenever several rows come from one source and the model will meet new sources: patients, customers, devices, schools, recording sessions. If one patient's visits sit on both sides of a split, the model can score well by recognizing the patient rather than learning the disease. The Build-along measures exactly how much that inflates a score. StratifiedGroupKFold does both jobs at once.

TimeSeriesSplit trains only on rows that come before the test block, the way the model will be used. It assumes rows are sorted by time. Two options matter in practice: gap= leaves out rows between training and test (useful when a feature uses the last few days of data), and test_size= fixes the length of each test window.

#Several metrics, and how much they move

cross_validate returns one row per fold, for as many metrics as you ask for, plus fit times and, optionally, training scores:

Report each metric as mean ± standard deviation across folds, and keep the per-fold table for later: comparing two models fold by fold (same folds for both) is far more sensitive than comparing their means. Two cautions about that standard deviation. The folds share most of their training rows, so the scores aren't independent, and the std understates the true uncertainty. And a big gap between train_ and test_ scores is your overfitting gauge; here the gap is small, which is what a well-regularized linear model looks like.

#When tuning is part of the model, you need two loops

GridSearchCV tries many settings and keeps the one with the best cross-validated score. That best score is the maximum of many noisy estimates, and a maximum of noisy numbers is biased upward. Reporting it as your model's performance is like reporting your best of twenty dice rolls as your average. Nested cross-validation wraps the whole search, tuning included, inside an outer loop whose test folds the search never sees:

Passing a GridSearchCV to cross_val_score is all it takes: each outer fold runs a complete search on its training part. The nested number answers the question you actually care about: how well does "tune an SVM this way, then train it" perform on new data? The best settings can differ between outer folds, and that's fine, since you're grading the procedure. To get a final model, run the search once on all the training data.

⚠️ Watch out

Passing groups= to the wrong splitter does nothing. cross_validate(model, X, y, groups=patients, cv=StratifiedKFold(5)) runs without an error, but StratifiedKFold ignores groups (scikit-learn only prints a UserWarning, which is easy to miss), so patients still straddle folds. Groups only take effect with a group-aware splitter such as GroupKFold.

⚠️ Watch out

TimeSeriesSplit trusts your row order. If the DataFrame isn't sorted by date, "the past" is a random mix and the scores mean nothing. Call df.sort_values("date") first, and check the date ranges of the first and last split.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A dataset has 2,000 X-rays from 400 patients (five each), and the model will be used on new patients. Which splitter?

  • It balances classes but scatters each patient's X-rays across folds, so the model can recognize patients it has already seen.

  • Every X-ray of a patient lands in the same fold, so each test fold contains only new patients, like real use.

  • Nothing here is about predicting later time periods from earlier ones.

Show answer

B. Every X-ray of a patient lands in the same fold, so each test fold contains only new patients, like real use.

2Shuffled KFold(5) on a dataset with 11 positives gives one test fold with zero positives. What happens to ROC AUC on that fold?

  • AUC compares positives with negatives; with no positives there's nothing to compare.

  • Stratifying keeps two or three positives in every fold and avoids the problem.

  • AUC and accuracy are different quantities; with one class present, AUC can't be computed.

Show answer

B. Stratifying keeps two or three positives in every fold and avoids the problem.

3GridSearchCV reports best_score_ = 0.89. Nested CV of the same search gives 0.86. Which number goes in your report, and why?

  • Selecting the maximum makes it optimistic; the outer folds in nested CV never influenced the choice.

  • It's the best score among the candidates, and the selection itself pushed it up.

  • Averaging an optimistic estimate with an honest one is still optimistic.

Show answer

A. Selecting the maximum makes it optimistic; the outer folds in nested CV never influenced the choice.

4Which use of cross_validate gives the most useful comparison between two models?

  • Different folds add noise to the comparison.

  • Identical folds mean the differences come from the models, not from which rows were tested.

  • One split gives one number per model; as the opening chart showed, that number depends on the split.

Show answer

B. Identical folds mean the differences come from the models, not from which rows were tested.

Key takeaways

  • One random split can flip a model comparison; cross-validation tests every row once and shows the spread.
  • Shuffle KFold unless row order means time; stratify classification folds, especially with a rare class.
  • Group rows that share a source (patient, customer, device) with GroupKFold, and respect time order with TimeSeriesSplit.
  • Use cross_validate for several metrics; report mean ± std, compare models fold by fold, and watch the train/test gap.
  • The best score of a search is optimistic. Nested CV grades the whole tune-then-train procedure.

#Further reading

  • Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance (opens in a new tab): the user guide, covering every splitter, cross_validate, and permutation tests.
  • Visualizing cross-validation behavior (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's own fold-grid plots for more splitters than shown here.
  • Nested versus non-nested cross-validation (opens in a new tab): repeats the comparison above many times to show how consistent the optimism is.

What you'll learn

  • Write a function that runs cross_validate and returns a tidy per-fold table.
  • Compare two models under row-level and patient-level cross-validation, and explain why the ranking flips.
  • Check programmatically that no patient appears in both the training and test part of a fold.

A clinic wants a model that flags a condition from routine visit measurements, and it will be used on new patients. The data has 601 visits from 60 patients, between 6 and 14 visits each. By the end you'll have a harness that produces this kind of table for any model and any splitter, and you'll know which of its rows to believe:

#Step 1: Generate the visits and look at their structure

Each patient has a personal baseline for six routine readings (think resting heart rate or a lab value that differs between people but barely changes between visits). Two markers carry the real, noisy signal. The diagnosis belongs to the patient, so it's the same at every visit.

Notice the readings: a patient's six values stay close to their baseline at every visit. That makes each patient recognizable, and that's the trap.

#Step 2: Write the harness

The harness takes a model and a splitter, always passes groups (non-group splitters simply ignore it), and returns one tidy row per fold. Returning a DataFrame instead of printing means every later step can filter, average, and plot the same table.

Silencing that one warning is deliberate and narrow: the harness passes groups to every splitter on purpose, and the warning would otherwise print once per call. Never silence warnings wholesale in a notebook; you'd lose the ones that matter.

#Step 3: Run both models under both schemes

Two candidates: a scaled logistic regression, and a k-nearest-neighbors classifier, which predicts from the most similar visits it has stored. Two schemes: shuffle the visits into folds, or keep each patient's visits together.

Read it twice. With visits shuffled, k-NN looks like the clear winner. With patients kept together, it's clearly the worse model, and both models lose ground. Same data, same models; only the question changed.

Here's what happened. When a patient's visits sit on both sides of a fold, k-NN finds that patient's other visits among the nearest neighbors (their baselines match) and copies their diagnosis. That's memorizing patients, not detecting a condition, and it's useless for a new patient. Logistic regression can't memorize individuals as easily, so it's hurt less. The group-aware scheme asks the question the clinic actually has.

#Step 4: Prove the folds are clean

Trust, then verify. For each fold, count the patients who appear on both sides:

With shuffled visits, nearly every test patient also has visits in training. With StratifiedGroupKFold, the overlap is zero in every fold. Keep a check like this in any project with grouped data; it takes four lines and catches a misconfigured splitter instantly.

#Step 5: Plot the folds, not just the means

The spread tells its own story. Under the honest scheme, k-NN's folds range widely, because with 12 patients per test fold, a handful of unusual patients can sink a fold. When fold scores vary this much, a single mean hides most of what you know.

#Step 6: Tune honestly with nested, group-aware CV

Both models have a setting worth tuning: k-NN's number of neighbors, and logistic regression's regularization strength C. Tuning has to respect patients too, in both loops, so we write the outer loop by hand and pass each outer training part's groups to the inner search:

Two things to read in those tables. First, the outer test folds never influenced the choice of C or k, so the means at the bottom are honest estimates of "tune, then train" for each model. Second, look at the chosen settings. Logistic regression picks the smallest C every time, and k-NN picks the largest k in four folds out of five, averaging over so many neighbors that one patient's other visits can't dominate. Both winners sit at the edge of their grids, which means the grids were too narrow; Module 4 deals with that. Tuning barely moved logistic regression (0.758 against 0.761 untuned) but recovered much of k-NN's score (0.725 against 0.614).

So which model? Logistic regression still leads, 0.758 to 0.725, but that gap is smaller than either model's fold-to-fold spread of about 0.05. A defensible recommendation says exactly that: logistic regression, because it's at least as accurate on new patients, simpler, and steadier across folds, with the note that tuned k-NN is close and that more patients would sharpen the comparison. Compare that with where we started: row-level CV would have shipped k-NN with a claimed AUC of 0.91.

#The finished program

Here's the whole harness in one cell, ready to reuse with another dataset: replace make_visits, the models dictionary, and the grids.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Under shuffled visits, k-NN scored about 0.91 AUC; under patient-level folds, about 0.61. Which number estimates performance for the clinic's new patients?

  • It's higher because test patients' other visits were in training, which won't happen with new patients.

  • The evaluation has to mirror deployment, and deployment means new patients.

  • Averaging with a leaky estimate just imports part of the leak.

Show answer

B. The evaluation has to mirror deployment, and deployment means new patients.

2Why does the nested loop pass groups=groups.iloc[train_idx] to search.fit?

  • Without it, the inner search would tune on leaky folds and favor settings that memorize patients, like small k.

  • It runs fine without them; it just tunes on the wrong kind of folds.

  • The outer splitter already handles stratification; this argument is about the inner search.

Show answer

A. Without it, the inner search would tune on leaky folds and favor settings that memorize patients, like small k.

3k-NN picked k=135, the largest value in the grid, in four of five outer folds. What should you do next?

  • You only know it's the best of the values you tried; larger values might be better still.

  • A best value on the edge of the grid means the search range was too narrow.

  • Nothing failed; the search is telling you where to look next.

Show answer

B. A best value on the edge of the grid means the search range was too narrow.

Key takeaways

  • A harness that returns a per-fold DataFrame makes every comparison filterable, plottable, and repeatable.
  • Shuffling rows from repeat patients (or customers, devices, schools) lets a model score by recognizing them, and can reverse a model ranking.
  • Verify group-aware folds with a set intersection; zero shared groups is the requirement.
  • Plot fold scores, not just means; a wide spread is information.
  • In nested CV with groups, both loops must be group-aware, so pass the training part's groups to the inner search.

#Extend it

What you'll learn

  • Predict how many model fits a cross-validated search will run.
  • Choose and configure the right splitter for grouped, rare-class, and time-ordered data.
  • Write a custom scorer with make_scorer and read scikit-learn's sign convention.
  • Know what cross_val_predict is for, and what it isn't.
  • Compare two models with paired, repeated folds instead of a single pair of means.

Run the setup cell first; every exercise builds on these imports.

#Warm-up: count the fits

cross_validate(GridSearchCV(model, grid, cv=5), X, y, cv=4), where grid has 3 values of one parameter and 4 of another. How many times is model fitted in total?

Show solution

Each search tries 3 × 4 = 12 candidates on 5 inner folds (60 fits), then refits the winner on its whole training part (1 more): 61 fits. The outer loop runs that search 4 times, so 244 fits. Multiply before you press run: at half a second per fit, that's two minutes, and a 10-value grid would make it twenty.

#Exercise 1: Match the splitter to the data

Write the splitter you'd use for each case, with its key arguments:

  1. 5,000 product reviews, one per customer, rating predicted as positive or negative (12% negative).
  2. 900 recordings of 30 speakers, classifying the spoken word; the model must work for new speakers.
  3. Daily electricity use for two years, predicting tomorrow; features include a 7-day rolling average.
  4. 40,000 house sales from one year, predicting price.
Need a hint?

Ask three questions in order: does time order matter, do rows share a source, and is it classification with uneven classes?

Show solution

The gap=7 in case 3 matters because the rolling average for the first test days is computed from days that are also in training; leaving a week out keeps the two parts apart. In case 4, if the same houses sold more than once, you'd group by house ID; and if the model will price next year's sales, a time-based split by sale date would be more honest still.

#Exercise 2: Why are my scores NaN?

The rows below are sorted by label (all negatives first), as happens when data is exported from a database ordered by outcome. Run the cross-validation, explain every nan, and fix it.

Need a hint?

Without shuffling, fold 1 is rows 0 to 39. What labels do those rows have? Now look at the training part of fold 5.

Show solution

Folds 1 to 4 contain only negatives, so AUC (which compares positives against negatives) is undefined there, and accuracy just measures how often the model says "negative". Fold 5's training part is rows 0 to 159, all negatives, so logistic regression can't even be fitted, and every metric for that fold is nan. By default, cross_validate records a failure as nan (error_score=np.nan) instead of stopping, which is why it's easy to miss. Shuffled, stratified folds fix both problems. Set error_score="raise" while developing if you'd rather fail loudly.

#Exercise 3: Validate a forecast the way it will be used

Below is a year of daily demand with a drifting level and a weekend bump. Features are yesterday's demand, the demand a week ago, a weekend flag, and the day number. Compare MAE from shuffled KFold(5) with TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=30, gap=7), and print the date range of each time-based split. Which estimate should you report for "predict tomorrow"?

Need a hint?

cross_val_score(..., scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error") returns negative numbers; flip the sign. For the date ranges, loop over TimeSeriesSplit(...).split(X3) and index demand["date"] with the train and test positions.

Show solution

Shuffled folds look better because the forest gets to train on the days on both sides of each test day and simply interpolates; it never has to deal with the level drifting somewhere new. A forest also can't extrapolate day_number beyond what it has seen, a weakness only the time-ordered split exposes. Report the TimeSeriesSplit number. The printout confirms each test month starts a week after training ends.

#Exercise 4: Score by what mistakes cost

In a fraud-review queue, a missed fraud (false negative) costs 5 units and a false alarm costs 1. Write a scorer for total cost with make_scorer, and cross-validate three models with accuracy, recall, and cost. Does the ranking change with the metric?

Need a hint?

Your cost function takes (y_true, y_pred); get the four counts with confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=[0, 1]).ravel(), which returns tn, fp, fn, tp. Lower cost is better, so pass greater_is_better=False, and expect scikit-learn to report the cost as a negative number.

Show solution

k-NN has the best accuracy and the worst cost: it rarely flags anything, which is cheap in accuracy terms (most rows are negative) and expensive when misses cost five times more. With greater_is_better=False, scikit-learn negates the score so that "higher is better" holds for every scorer; that's why test_cost came back negative. Choosing the metric is choosing the winner, so write the metric down before you compare models.

#Exercise 5: Out-of-fold predictions are for looking, not for scoring

Use cross_val_predict to get a prediction for every diabetes patient from a model that never saw that patient, and plot predicted against actual. Then compute R² on those pooled predictions and compare it with the mean of the per-fold R² from cross_val_score on the same folds. Why do they differ?

Need a hint?

Use one KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) object for both calls. from sklearn.metrics import r2_score.

Show solution

The two numbers measure different things. Per-fold R² compares each fold's predictions with that fold's mean; pooled R² compares all predictions with the overall mean, mixing predictions from five different models. scikit-learn's documentation warns against reporting the pooled number as a generalization score. Out-of-fold predictions shine for plots like this one, for error analysis (which patients are badly predicted?), and as inputs to later steps such as stacking.

#Exercise 6: Is logistic regression really better than k-NN?

On the make_classification data from the Notes lesson (n_samples=300, n_features=10, n_informative=4, n_redundant=2, flip_y=0.08, random_state=5), score both models from the Notes on the same 50 splits from RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=10, random_state=0). Compute the per-split difference, plot its distribution, and count wins, losses, and ties.

Need a hint?

Pass the same RepeatedStratifiedKFold object to both cross_val_score calls; because its seed is an integer, both get identical splits, so scores_a - scores_b pairs up correctly.

Show solution

Logistic regression wins clearly more often than it loses, and the average edge is a couple of points. Pairing is what makes this visible: each difference cancels out how easy or hard that particular test fold was. One caution before reaching for a t-test: the 50 differences aren't independent (the splits share training rows), so a standard t-test overstates confidence. If you need a p-value, use a test corrected for this, such as the Nadeau–Bengio corrected t-test, or simply report the win rate and the spread.

#Challenge: How optimistic is best_score_?

The Notes showed one search whose best_score_ beat its nested estimate. Is that a fluke? For 6 different small datasets (make_classification(n_samples=120, n_features=8, n_informative=3, flip_y=0.1, random_state=seed)), run a GridSearchCV over an SVM's C in [0.1, 1, 10] and gamma in [0.01, 0.1, 1], record best_score_, then compute the nested estimate with a 5-fold outer loop. Plot one against the other and report the average gap.

Need a hint?

Use different seeds for the inner and outer splitters. A scatter plot with a diagonal line makes the pattern obvious: points above the line are searches that oversold themselves.

Show solution

On average the search's own best score sits above the nested estimate, as theory predicts: it is the maximum over nine noisy candidates evaluated on the same folds. Individual datasets can land below the line (with 120 rows, every estimate is noisy), which is why one comparison proves little and a repeated experiment like this one tells you more. The bias grows with the number of candidates you try and shrinks with more data.

What you'll learn

  • Estimate the cost of a search (candidates × folds × seconds per fit) before running it.
  • Explain why random search finds good values of the settings that matter faster than a grid.
  • Choose distributions such as loguniform and randint, and know when a list is the better choice.
  • Use HalvingRandomSearchCV and early stopping to spend compute only on promising candidates.
  • Recognize when repeated searching has started fitting noise in the validation folds.

Here is a grid that looks modest for a gradient-boosted model: five learning rates, five tree sizes, four leaf sizes, four regularization strengths, three iteration counts.

Almost an hour, for one model, before you've looked at a single result. And the cost isn't only time. The winner is whichever of 1,200 noisy cross-validation scores came out highest, so part of its lead is luck. This lesson is about spending a search budget where it counts, and about not fooling yourself with the result.

#Count before you search

The cost of any search is candidates × folds × seconds per fit, plus one refit at the end. Time one fit first (%time model.fit(X, y) in Colab), then size the search to the minutes you're willing to wait. Grids grow multiplicatively: adding one more 4-value setting to the grid above turns 1,200 into 4,800. So the first decision is how many candidates to try, and the second is which ones.

#Random search covers what matters

Usually only one or two hyperparameters drive most of the score, and you don't know in advance which. A 3 × 3 grid tests only three distinct values of each setting; nine random points test nine distinct values of each. In the picture below, setting a matters (the score peaks sharply near 0.72) and setting b barely does.

This is the argument from Bergstra and Bengio's 2012 paper on random search, and it's why RandomizedSearchCV with a fixed n_iter is the sensible default. It also makes the budget a single number you choose, independent of how many settings you search over.

#Sample on the scale where the setting acts

Settings like C, alpha, learning_rate, and regularization strengths act multiplicatively: going from 0.001 to 0.01 matters about as much as going from 0.1 to 1. Sampling them uniformly wastes nearly every draw on the top decade.

The rules of thumb: loguniform(low, high) for positive settings that act by factors; randint(low, high) for integers on a linear scale (note that high is excluded); uniform(loc, scale) for fractions such as max_features (careful: the second argument is the width, not the upper end). For integers that act on a log scale, like a minimum leaf size, a plain list of log-spaced values works well, because RandomizedSearchCV samples lists uniformly. Here's a randomized search of a decision tree using all four:

An unpruned tree memorizes noise (this data has 10% flipped labels); the search finds depth, leaf size, and pruning that generalize.

#Successive halving: cheap auditions, expensive callbacks

Most random candidates are clearly bad, and you can tell that from a small sample of the data. Successive halving evaluates many candidates on a few rows, keeps the best third (with factor=3), triples their rows, and repeats until a handful compete on all the data.

Three times the candidates for roughly the same time as the random search above. The import line is required because the halving classes are still marked experimental. Two settings matter: min_resources (too small, and early rounds are pure noise; some models can't even fit on a dozen rows) and factor. Halving's risk is that a setting which only shines with lots of data, like a deep tree, gets eliminated in round one.

#Early stopping: let the model choose its own length

For boosting, the number of iterations is a hyperparameter you shouldn't search at all. With early_stopping=True, HistGradientBoostingClassifier holds out validation_fraction of the training rows (10% by default) and stops once the validation loss hasn't improved for n_iter_no_change rounds. The curve shows why:

So set max_iter generously as a ceiling, turn early stopping on, and spend your search on the learning rate and tree shape instead. Check n_iter_ afterwards: if it equals max_iter, the ceiling was too low. One detail: on datasets under 10,000 rows the default early_stopping="auto" means off, so switch it on explicitly.

#Every search peeks at the same folds

Each candidate you score is a look at the validation folds, and the best of many looks is biased upward, even when there's nothing to find. Here a random search runs on data whose labels are pure coin flips:

Real searches have the same bias on top of real signal, and so do you, every time you rerun a search after looking at the results. Three defenses: keep the search modest, estimate the final model with nested CV or an untouched test set, and decide the search space before you see the scores.

⚠️ Watch out

Inside a pipeline, parameter names need the step prefix. Searching {"C": ...} on make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()) fails with ValueError: Invalid parameter 'C' for estimator Pipeline(...). The name is logisticregression__C (step name, two underscores, parameter). Print sorted(pipe.get_params()) to see every valid name.

⚠️ Watch out

best_score_ is not your model's performance. It's the maximum over every candidate you tried, on the folds used to pick it. Report a nested-CV estimate or a test-set score instead.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A random search samples C from uniform(0.001, 100). Roughly what share of candidates have C below 1?

  • Half the draws would be below 50 on a uniform scale, not below 1.

  • A uniform draw from a range 100 wide lands below 1 about 1% of the time, so small values are almost never tried. Use loguniform(0.001, 100) instead.

  • That's what loguniform would give; a uniform distribution ignores decades.

Show answer

B. A uniform draw from a range 100 wide lands below 1 about 1% of the time, so small values are almost never tried. Use loguniform(0.001, 100) instead.

2A grid search over four settings with 5 values each, 5-fold CV, at 0.4 s per fit. How long will it take?

  • That counts 20 values, but grids multiply: 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 625 candidates.

  • 625 candidates × 5 folds × 0.4 s = 1,250 s, plus a final refit.

  • Check the multiplication: 625 × 5 = 3,125 fits.

Show answer

B. 625 candidates × 5 folds × 0.4 s = 1,250 s, plus a final refit.

3After early stopping, model.n_iter_ equals max_iter. What does that tell you?

  • Early stopping never triggered; the model may want more iterations.

  • When it triggers, n_iter_ is below max_iter.

  • Overfitting would make validation loss rise, which triggers early stopping.

Show answer

A. Early stopping never triggered; the model may want more iterations.

4You run HalvingRandomSearchCV on a HistGradientBoostingClassifier(early_stopping=True) with the default min_resources, and every fit fails with an error saying a test size of 1 is smaller than the number of classes. Why?

  • It does; the problem is the size of the first round.

  • Set min_resources to a size the model can actually learn from, such as a few hundred rows.

  • The factor sets how fast rows grow per round; the problem starts in round one.

Show answer

B. Set min_resources to a size the model can actually learn from, such as a few hundred rows.

Key takeaways

  • Cost = candidates × folds × seconds per fit. Count it before you run anything.
  • Random search with a fixed n_iter covers the settings that matter better than a grid with the same budget.
  • Sample multiplicative settings with loguniform; use randint or lists for integers.
  • Successive halving auditions many candidates on few rows; set min_resources sensibly.
  • Use early stopping instead of searching over the number of boosting iterations.
  • The best score of a search is biased upward, more so the more candidates you try. Grade the final choice on data the search never saw.

#Further reading

  • Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator (opens in a new tab): the user guide for every search class, including successive halving and how factor and min_resources interact.
  • Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization (opens in a new tab): Bergstra and Bengio's paper, the source of the grid-versus-random argument.
  • Early stopping in gradient boosting (opens in a new tab): scikit-learn's example comparing training time and error with and without it.
