m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a time budget into a number of search candidates.
  • Use early stopping and read a model's training and validation curves.
  • Search a pipeline's hyperparameters with sensible distributions and prefixed names.
  • Read cv_results_ to spot a search range that's too narrow, and a validation curve to spot a plateau.
  • Decide whether a tuning gain is real by comparing folds, before touching the test set.

Module 2's churn model reached its best score with hand-built features. Gradient boosting can learn curves and interactions by itself, but it has more settings, and every setting is a temptation to search too long. The goal here is a disciplined run that fits inside about 15 seconds of compute:

#Step 1: Data, pipeline, and two baselines

The same streaming-service generator as Module 2, with 2,000 customers. The pipeline keeps only the two simplest engineered features (tenure and log hours per device); boosting has to discover the rest. HistGradientBoostingClassifier handles missing values natively, so the numeric columns pass straight through with no imputer or scaler.

Two things to keep from this cell: the default boosted model already beats logistic regression on these features, and one fit takes a fraction of a second. The pipeline step is named boost, so every hyperparameter in the search below will be spelled boost__<name>.

#Step 2: Let early stopping choose the number of trees

Fit once and look inside the boosting step. With early_stopping=True, it set aside 10% of the training rows and recorded the loss on both parts after every iteration.

The scores are stored as negative loss (so that higher is better everywhere in scikit-learn), hence the minus signs. The model stopped far below its ceiling of 500, so max_iter doesn't need tuning, and the search can spend its budget elsewhere. The growing gap between the curves is normal for boosting; what matters is that the validation curve has flattened.

#Step 3: Size the search to a budget

Say you're willing to spend about 10 seconds on the search. From Step 1, a fit takes well under a second, and early stopping will keep most candidates short.

The formula is the one from the Notes, solved for the number of candidates. Your machine will print a different number, which is the point: the budget, not the candidate count, is what you decide.

#Step 4: Run the randomized search

Four settings shape the trees: the learning rate (multiplicative, so loguniform), the number of leaves per tree (an integer, randint), the minimum rows per leaf (an integer on a log scale, so a list), and L2 regularization (loguniform).

min(n_iter, 12) caps the search so the lesson stays quick even on a fast machine. The winner trains slowly (small learning rate) with small trees, a common pattern on a dataset this size.

#Step 5: Read the search, not just the winner

cv_results_ holds every candidate's settings and fold scores. Two questions to ask of it: did the winner sit at the edge of a range, and how flat is the top?

Look at the std_test_score column next to the means: the top few candidates differ by less than their own fold-to-fold spread. That's a plateau, and it's good news, because it means the exact values don't matter much. If instead the best dots had crowded against an end of the axis, the right move would be to widen that range and search again.

A validation curve checks one setting more carefully: hold the others at the winner's values and sweep just that one.

#Step 6: Is the gain real?

The search compared every candidate on the same three folds as the baseline (same splitter, same integer seed), so the winner's per-fold scores pair up with the defaults' per-fold scores:

Tuning helped on every fold, by about a point of AUC. Remember Module 3, though: the winner was selected using these very folds, so this gain is a little optimistic. It's still the right check to make before spending more compute; if the gain had been mixed in sign, the honest decision would be to keep the defaults.

#Step 7: Open the test set once

The ordering matches cross-validation: tuned boosting first, then the defaults, then logistic regression. The test gaps are small, and with 500 test customers, a difference under about 0.01 is within the noise. The honest summary: tuning was worth doing because it was cheap and consistent across folds, and it is not a dramatic improvement. In Module 2 the hand-built age gap and first-year interaction did more for logistic regression than this whole search did for boosting, a useful reminder that features usually matter more than settings.

#The finished program

Once tuning is done, freeze the chosen settings (rounded) in the training code and stop searching. This cell trains the final model from scratch with them. Rounding nudges the result in the third decimal place, and that's fine: on the plateau, nearby settings behave alike.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why didn't the search include max_iter?

  • With early stopping on, max_iter is only a ceiling. Searching it would waste candidates.

  • It caps the number of trees, which matters a lot without early stopping.

  • max_leaf_nodes is an integer and was searched with randint.

Show answer

A. With early stopping on, max_iter is only a ceiling. Searching it would waste candidates.

2The top five candidates' mean AUCs differ by 0.003, and each has a fold std of about 0.015. What should you conclude?

  • Differences far smaller than the fold-to-fold spread can't separate the candidates.

  • A flat top means the model isn't sensitive to these settings in that region, which makes the choice robust.

  • Nothing failed; a plateau is a common and useful finding.

Show answer

B. A flat top means the model isn't sensitive to these settings in that region, which makes the choice robust.

3Why compare tuned and default scores fold by fold rather than just comparing their means?

  • They can; pairing adds information the means hide.

  • If the gain has the same sign on every fold, it's more convincing than a small difference in means.

  • It doesn't; the winner was chosen on these folds, so a small optimism remains.

Show answer

B. If the gain has the same sign on every fold, it's more convincing than a small difference in means.

Key takeaways

  • Decide a time budget, then derive the number of candidates from seconds per fit and folds.
  • Turn on early stopping and search learning rate and tree shape instead of the number of trees.
  • In a pipeline, every searched name carries the step prefix (boost__learning_rate).
  • Read cv_results_: winners at the edge mean widen the range; a flat top means stop searching.
  • Check a tuning gain fold by fold before you trust it, then open the test set once.

#Extend it

  • Replace RandomizedSearchCV with HalvingRandomSearchCV(n_candidates=36, factor=3, min_resources=150). Is it faster here? With fits this quick, the overhead of many small rounds can cancel the savings; halving shines when single fits take seconds.
  • Add Module 2's new_with_issues and age_gap features to the boosted pipeline. Does boosting still benefit, or had it already learned them?
  • Estimate the tuned model honestly with nested CV: pass the whole RandomizedSearchCV to cross_val_score with a 3-fold outer loop.

  • Validation curves (opens in a new tab): the user guide for validation_curve and learning_curve, with how to read under- and overfitting.

What you'll learn

  • Write a search space that swaps entire pipeline steps, and count its candidates.
  • Predict the values randint, uniform, and loguniform produce, including their boundary rules.
  • Use a callable refit to prefer simpler models whose score is statistically tied with the best.
  • Predict the rounds of a successive-halving search before running it.
  • Detect a too-narrow search range and fix it.
  • Explain, with numbers, why choosing settings by test score inflates that score.

Run the setup cell first.

#Warm-up: count a grid with alternatives

param_grid can be a list of dictionaries; the search tries each dictionary's combinations and adds them up. How many candidates does this have, and how many fits with cv=5?

Show solution

4 × 2 = 8 from the first dictionary plus 3 from the second: 11 candidates, so 55 fits plus 1 refit. Lists add; values inside one dictionary multiply. (As written, the second dictionary would fail, since n_neighbors isn't a logistic regression setting. Exercise 1 shows how to swap the model itself.)

#Exercise 1: Search over model families, not just settings

Build Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", LogisticRegression())]) and one GridSearchCV that compares three families, each with its own settings: logistic regression with C in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10], k-NN with n_neighbors in [5, 15, 45], and a decision tree with max_depth in [3, 5, 8] and the scaler turned off. Print the candidate count, the best candidate, and the best score for each family.

Need a hint?

A whole step can be a searched value: {"model": [KNeighborsClassifier()], "model__n_neighbors": [...]}. Setting "scale": ["passthrough"] turns the scaler off for that dictionary. To get each family's best, group cv_results_ by the type of param_model.

Show solution

Ten candidates, one consistent set of folds, one table. Because every family is scored on the same folds, the comparison is fair, and the search refits the overall winner automatically. Turning the scaler off for the tree is tidy rather than necessary, since trees ignore scale.

#Exercise 2: What do these distributions really produce?

Before running anything, predict: (a) can randint(2, 64) ever produce 64? (b) what range does uniform(0.1, 0.9) cover? (c) roughly what share of loguniform(1e-4, 1e2) draws fall below 1? Then check all three with 10,000 draws each.

Need a hint?

scipy's randint(low, high) follows Python's range. scipy's uniform(loc, scale) covers [loc, loc + scale]. A log-uniform distribution gives every factor of ten the same share.

Show solution

(a) No: the upper bound is excluded, so the largest value is 63. Write randint(2, 65) if you mean 64. (b) 0.1 to 1.0, not 0.1 to 0.9: the second argument is the width. This is the most common distribution bug in tuning code. (c) Four of the six decades lie below 1, so about 67%.

#Exercise 3: Prefer the simplest model that ties with the best

Grid-search a decision tree's max_depth over 1 to 14, scored by accuracy. Instead of keeping the top scorer, keep the shallowest tree whose mean score is within one standard error of the best (the one-standard-error rule). Write it as a function and pass it as refit=. Compare the depth it picks with the raw best depth, and plot the mean score with error bars.

Need a hint?

A callable refit receives cv_results_ and must return an index. Standard error = std_test_score / sqrt(n_splits). Find the best mean, compute its threshold, then choose the smallest depth whose mean clears it.

Show solution

When several settings tie within noise, the simpler one is the safer bet: it has fewer ways to have fit quirks of these particular folds. Note that with a callable refit, the search has no best_score_; read the chosen candidate's score from cv_results_ instead.

#Exercise 4: Learning rate versus number of trees

With early stopping on and max_iter=1000, fit HistGradientBoostingClassifier with learning rates 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, and 1.0 on a 75/25 split. For each, record n_iter_, fit time, and held-out AUC, and plot the validation loss curves on one chart. What trade-off do you see?

Need a hint?

model.validation_score_ holds negative log loss per iteration; plot its negative. Time each fit with time.perf_counter(). Score with roc_auc_score(y_hold, model.predict_proba(X_hold)[:, 1]).

Show solution

Smaller learning rates take smaller steps, so they need many more trees and more time, and they usually end up as good or slightly better. Very large rates overshoot and stop early at a worse loss. In practice: pick a moderate rate (0.05 to 0.2), let early stopping set the length, and only shrink the rate if you have time to spare.

#Exercise 5: Predict the halving rounds

A HalvingRandomSearchCV gets n_candidates=40, factor=2, min_resources=100, on 1,600 rows. Write down how many rounds it will run, and how many candidates and rows each round uses. Then run it with a cheap decision tree and compare with n_candidates_ and n_resources_.

Need a hint?

Rows multiply by factor each round until they would pass 1,600. Candidates are divided by factor each round, rounded up.

Show solution

Rows double from 100 to 1,600 (100, 200, 400, 800, 1,600): five rounds. Candidates halve, rounding up: 40, 20, 10, 5, 3. The final round compares three finalists on all the data. A smaller factor means more, gentler rounds; a larger one eliminates aggressively.

#Exercise 6: The winner on the edge

A teammate grid-searches k-NN's n_neighbors over 1 to 9 and reports "best k = 9". Rerun their search, notice the problem, then draw a validation curve over a much wider range (1 to 200, log-spaced) and report a better k.

Need a hint?

The grid's largest value is 9, so "best k = 9" can't tell you whether larger is better. For the curve, np.unique(np.logspace(0, np.log10(200), 12).astype(int)) gives log-spaced integers.

Show solution

A winner at the boundary of the search space means "at least this much, maybe more". With 12% flipped labels, small k fits the noise; the curve keeps improving past 9 and peaks in the high teens, before averaging over too many neighbors starts to blur the classes. Add an edge check to every search: if a numeric best value equals the range's minimum or maximum, widen the range and run again.

#Challenge: What tuning on the test set costs

Simulate it. From one large pool of generated data, take 300 training rows, 300 "test" rows, and 5,000 "future" rows that stand in for real use. Sample 40 random decision-tree settings. Method A picks the setting with the best test score; method B picks the best 5-fold CV score on the training rows. For each method, compare the score it claims (test score or CV score) with its real score on the future rows. Repeat over 5 seeds and report the average optimism (claimed minus future).

Need a hint?

For each seed: draw the pool with make_classification(n_samples=5600, ..., random_state=seed) and slice it. Use ParameterSampler(space, n_iter=40, random_state=seed) to get the 40 settings. For B you can simply run RandomizedSearchCV on the training rows with the same 40 settings via n_iter=40, random_state=seed.

Show solution

Both claims are optimistic, because both are the maximum of 40 noisy scores. Method A's test score was supposed to be the untouched, honest number, and choosing by it spent that honesty: what remains is a selection score like any other, measured on fewer rows (300 versus 5 folds of 60 that cover all 300), so it's typically the noisier and more inflated of the two. Method B leaves the test set unused, so you can still score the chosen model on it once and get an unbiased estimate. That's the whole argument for keeping the test set sealed until the end.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why ROC AUC barely reacts to class imbalance while average precision does, and compute average precision by hand.
  • Describe what class_weight="balanced" changes inside a model, and what it leaves alone.
  • Explain random oversampling, undersampling, and SMOTE, and where resampling must happen during cross-validation.
  • Choose a decision threshold from the cost of a false alarm and a miss, using TunedThresholdClassifierCV.
  • Combine models with VotingClassifier and StackingClassifier, and say when that helps.

Here is an experiment that surprises most people. Take a classifier's scores for 500 positive examples and freeze them. Then keep adding negatives drawn from the same distribution as before: 500, then 2,000, then 10,000, then 50,000. The model hasn't changed at all. Watch what two popular metrics say about it.

ROC AUC drifts from 0.911 to 0.896. Average precision (AP) collapses from 0.914 to 0.185. Both are telling the truth; they answer different questions.

#Why ROC AUC hardly notices the pile of negatives

The ROC curve's x-axis is the false positive rate: false alarms divided by all negatives. When the negatives grow from 500 to 50,000, a 2% false positive rate goes from 10 false alarms to 1,000. The rate is unchanged, so ROC AUC is unchanged. The person reading the alerts, though, now wades through 1,000 false alarms to find a few hundred real cases.

Precision is the metric that feels that pile: true positives divided by everything flagged. Average precision walks down the ranked list from the most confident prediction and averages the precision at each point where a new true positive is found. A model that guesses at random scores an AP equal to the positive share (0.01 when 1% are positive), so always compare AP to the prevalence, not to 0.5.

The fourth positive shows up at rank 7, when only 4 of the 7 flags are real, so it contributes 0.571. The scikit-learn function average_precision_score gives the same 0.830 for these items when no two scores tie.

#What class_weight="balanced" really changes

Now a realistic dataset: 3,000 parts off a production line, about 4.6% of them defective. class_weight="balanced" gives each class a weight of n_samples / (2 * n_in_class), so every defect counts about 21 times as much as a good part in the loss.

Look at the columns that measure ranking: AP and ROC AUC are almost identical, and the two models order the test parts with a rank correlation of 0.97. What changed is the scale. The average predicted probability jumped from about 0.05 (the real defect rate) to about 0.23, so far more parts cross the default 0.5 cutoff and recall rises.

For logistic regression, reweighting mostly slides the intercept, which is the same thing as moving the threshold. For trees and forests it can do more, because the weights change which split looks purest, so the ranking itself can shift. Either way, the probabilities a weighted model prints are no longer the chance of a defect. Module 7 shows how to repair them.

📝 Note

class_weight="balanced" is shorthand for passing sample_weight to fit, with each row getting its class's weight. Fitting the plain pipeline with logisticregression__sample_weight=weights[y_train] produces exactly the same coefficients.

#Resampling: copy rows, drop rows, or invent rows

Instead of weighting rows, you can change which rows the model sees.

  • Random oversampling repeats positives until the classes balance. For many models this behaves like integer weights, but flexible models such as k-NN or deep trees can memorize the copies.
  • Random undersampling throws away negatives. Training gets fast, but you discard information, so it is often repeated on many different subsamples whose models are then averaged.
  • SMOTE creates synthetic positives on the line between a positive and one of its nearest positive neighbours. It lives in the separate imbalanced-learn library (pip install imbalanced-learn in Colab), whose imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline applies samplers during fit only.

For a strong model judged by a ranking metric such as AP, resampling often adds little beyond what a plain model with a well-chosen threshold already gives, so test it with cross-validation instead of assuming it helps. What is never optional is where it happens.

#Choose the threshold from what each mistake costs

Suppose a missed defect costs the factory 20 times as much as an unnecessary inspection. If a model's probabilities are trustworthy, flagging a part pays off whenever p × 20 > (1 − p) × 1, which means p > 1/21 ≈ 0.048. That is the textbook optimum, and it is far below 0.5.

TunedThresholdClassifierCV finds the threshold empirically: it cross-validates the model, tries 100 cutoffs on each validation fold, and keeps the one with the best score. Give it the cost as a scorer (negated, because it maximizes).

The plain model's tuned threshold (about 0.11) sits in the same low range as the textbook 0.048, and both cut its cost well below what the 0.5 default costs. The balanced model wants a threshold near 0.59, and the textbook 1/21 is a disaster for it, because its "probabilities" are inflated. Once each model has its own tuned threshold their costs (281 and 251) are close, and with only about 41 defects in the test set that gap is within noise. The lesson: tune the threshold for whichever model you deploy, and only use cost formulas on probabilities you have checked.

#Two ways to combine models: voting and stacking

A single model has blind spots. Different kinds of model often have different blind spots, so combining them can cancel some errors.

  • Soft voting (VotingClassifier(voting="soft")) averages the members' predict_proba. Hard voting takes a majority of predicted labels and throws away confidence, so soft is usually better when every member gives probabilities.
  • Stacking (StackingClassifier) trains a small final estimator on the members' predictions. To keep that honest, it builds those predictions with internal cross-validation (cv=5 by default), so the final model learns from out-of-fold predictions, never from a member grading its own homework.

The three members are about equally good (AP near 0.71) and very different in how they work: a linear boundary, a neighbourhood vote, and a forest of axis-aligned splits. Both ensembles beat all three by about 0.03. The standard deviations are large, though, because each validation fold holds only about 27 defects. Before you claim the ensemble wins, compare the models fold by fold on the same splits, as you'll do in the Build-along.

⚠️ Watch out

Three ways rare-class work goes wrong.

  1. Resampling before splitting. If you oversample the whole dataset and then cross-validate, copies of the same positive sit in training and validation folds. k-NN and deep trees "recognize" them and the scores soar. Resample inside the fold, or use imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline.
  2. Picking the threshold on the test set. The threshold is a hyperparameter. Choose it with cross-validation on the training data, as TunedThresholdClassifierCV does, then check it once on the test set.
  3. Reading a weighted model's predict_proba as a real probability. After class_weight="balanced", a printed 0.6 might correspond to a true defect rate of 0.1.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model's scores stay the same, but the test set now has ten times as many negatives. What happens to its ROC AUC and AP?

  • ROC AUC divides false alarms by the number of negatives, so adding negatives from the same distribution leaves it about where it was.

  • The false positive rate is unchanged, but the count of false alarms grows tenfold, so precision at every recall level falls.

  • The model didn't change, but AP depends on how many negatives compete with each positive in the ranked list.

Show answer

B. The false positive rate is unchanged, but the count of false alarms grows tenfold, so precision at every recall level falls.

2You switch a logistic regression to class_weight="balanced". Which change should you expect?

  • For logistic regression the weights mostly shift the intercept; the ordering of examples barely moves, so AP stays close.

  • The weighting pushes every score toward the rare class, which is why recall at 0.5 rises and the probabilities stop matching real rates.

  • Weights change the loss for any model that accepts them; here they move the intercept a long way.

Show answer

B. The weighting pushes every score toward the rare class, which is why recall at 0.5 rises and the probabilities stop matching real rates.

3Missing a positive costs 9 and a false alarm costs 1, and the model's probabilities are well calibrated. Where should the threshold go?

  • That would flag only very confident cases, the opposite of what an expensive miss calls for.

  • 0.5 is right only when both mistakes cost the same.

  • Flag when p × 9 > (1 − p) × 1, which gives p > 1/10.

Show answer

C. Flag when p × 9 > (1 − p) × 1, which gives p > 1/10.

4Why does StackingClassifier use internal cross-validation to build the inputs for its final estimator?

  • In-sample predictions are overconfident, so a final model trained on them would trust whichever member overfits most.

  • Stacking doesn't tune the members; put a search object in as a member if you want that.

  • VotingClassifier simply averages fitted members and uses no internal cross-validation.

Show answer

A. In-sample predictions are overconfident, so a final model trained on them would trust whichever member overfits most.

Key takeaways

  • When positives are rare, report AP (and compare it with the positive share) or a cost, not accuracy or ROC AUC alone.
  • class_weight and resampling mostly move the decision boundary toward the rare class; they rarely improve how well a model ranks, and they distort its probabilities.
  • Resampling belongs inside each training fold, never before the split.
  • A threshold is a decision about costs. Tune it with cross-validation on training data, and check it once on the test set.
  • Soft voting and stacking help when the members are similarly strong and make different mistakes.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Tuning the decision threshold (opens in a new tab): the user guide behind TunedThresholdClassifierCV and FixedThresholdClassifier, with a cost-sensitive worked example.
  • Saito and Rehmsmeier (2015), The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot (opens in a new tab): the classic paper on why ROC curves flatter models on imbalanced data.
  • imbalanced-learn user guide (opens in a new tab): over- and undersampling methods, SMOTE variants, and the pipeline that applies them safely.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a balanced dataset into a realistic rare-class problem and seal a test set before modelling.
  • Compare several model families on identical folds with average precision, and read the fold-by-fold numbers.
  • Measure whether models make different mistakes before you combine them.
  • Build and compare a soft-voting and a stacking ensemble.
  • Tune the decision threshold for a recall-heavy goal, then evaluate everything once on the test set.

The digits dataset that ships with scikit-learn has 1,797 tiny 8×8 handwritten digits, about 180 of each. That balance is unusual. Real detection problems look more like "find the few interesting items in a big pile", so we'll recreate one: keep only 80 of the 8s, and build a model whose job is to flag them. The 8 is a good choice because it looks like a 3, a 9, and a 0 when written carelessly.

Here is the plan for the whole notebook.

#Step 1: Make the 8s rare and lock away a test set

We remove a random subset of the 8s (with a fixed seed so the run repeats), relabel the problem as "8 or not", and split off a stratified test set right away. The original digit labels ride along in the split so we can inspect mistakes later. Nothing below touches X_test until Step 7.

About 4.7% of the images are now 8s. With 56 eights in training, each of five folds will see roughly 11 of them, so expect noisy fold scores.

#Step 2: Score four different models on the same folds

Every model gets the same StratifiedKFold object, so they are graded on identical rows. The scaled models sit inside pipelines, so the scaler is refit inside every fold. The DummyClassifier shows the floor: its AP equals the share of 8s.

The SVC ranks best (AP about 0.92), and the forest's recall at the default threshold is only about 0.23 even though its AP is decent. That gap between "ranks well" and "flags enough at 0.5" is the pattern from the Notes, and it tells you the threshold, not the model, is the first thing to fix.

#Step 3: Do class weights help here?

Three of the four models accept class_weight. Let's see what it buys.

Recall at 0.5 jumps for logistic regression and the SVC, but AP stays within a couple of hundredths, and for logistic regression it even drops. The weights moved the line without making the models better at telling 8s from everything else. We'll keep the unweighted models, which also keeps their probabilities meaningful, and fix recall with a tuned threshold in Step 6.

#Step 4: Check that the models fail in different ways

An ensemble of four models that make the same mistakes is just one model, four times slower. cross_val_predict gives every training image a probability from a model that never saw it, so we can compare the members' out-of-fold scores directly.

The k-NN scores correlate only about 0.4 with the others, so it sees the problem differently from the three models that draw smooth boundaries. Each model misses between 8 and 43 of the 56 eights at 0.5, but only a handful are missed by all four. Those few are the ones no ensemble can rescue; every other miss is a chance for a teammate to cover.

#Step 5: Combine the models, and compare fold by fold

Now the two ensembles from the Notes. Because they use the same cv object as the members in Step 2, we can line their scores up fold by fold.

Both ensembles average about 0.94, ahead of the best member's 0.92, and they beat the best single model in most individual folds. That fold-level view is stronger evidence than the means alone, because each fold is a paired comparison on the same rows.

Which members does the stack trust? Its final estimator is a logistic regression, so its coefficients are the weights it gives each member's probability.

It leans most on k-NN and the SVC, the two strongest and least similar members. Since the vote and the stack score the same, we'll take the soft vote forward: it is simpler to explain and trains about five times faster, because it has no internal cross-validation.

#Step 6: Tune the threshold for a recall-heavy goal

Suppose every flagged image goes to a person who checks it, and missing an 8 is worse than an extra check. The F-beta score with beta=2 treats recall as twice as important as precision, which captures that preference in one number. TunedThresholdClassifierCV searches for the cutoff that maximizes it, using its own internal folds on the training data.

The chosen cutoff is about 0.2: an image only needs a one-in-five ensemble probability to be flagged. Because the vote's members are unweighted, that probability is still on a sensible scale.

#Step 7: Open the test set once

Everything is decided: the members, the ensemble, and the threshold. Now, and only now, we score the 511 sealed test images, comparing the ensemble with the best single model.

Out of 511 test images the detector flags 23, gets 22 of them right, and misses 2 of the 24 eights. Test AP (in the legend) is close to the cross-validated estimate, which is what you hope to see when nothing leaked. Notice, too, that the test set barely separates the ensemble from the SVC: with only 24 eights, one image more or less moves AP by a few hundredths. The fold-by-fold comparison in Step 5 is the stronger evidence for the ensemble; the test set's job is to confirm that nothing broke.

Numbers are not the end of an evaluation. Look at the mistakes.

The false alarm is a heavy, blobby 1 that only just crossed the cutoff (0.20 against a threshold of 0.197). The two missed 8s barely look like 8s: one is a squiggle and the other is almost a single stroke. A person would hesitate over these too, so they are hard cases rather than evidence that the model latched onto something strange.

#The finished program

Here is the whole detector in one cell, without the exploration: the data, the four members, the soft vote, the tuned threshold, and the single test evaluation.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 3, class_weight="balanced" raised the SVC's recall at 0.5 from about 0.68 to 0.89. Why did we still keep the unweighted SVC?

  • They can; any classifier with predict_proba can be a soft-voting member.

  • Weighting and thresholding both move the decision line; only the threshold leaves the probabilities on their real scale for averaging.

  • Recall matters a lot here, which is why Step 6 tunes for F2.

Show answer

B. Weighting and thresholding both move the decision line; only the threshold leaves the probabilities on their real scale for averaging.

2Why did Step 4 look at correlations between the members' out-of-fold scores before building any ensemble?

  • Step 2 already ranked the members by AP; correlation measures something else.

  • Four models with near-identical scores would average to the same ranking, so the ensemble would gain nothing.

  • There is no such rule; correlated members are allowed, they just add little.

Show answer

B. Four models with near-identical scores would average to the same ranking, so the ensemble would gain nothing.

3The tuned threshold came out at about 0.2. What would choosing it by maximizing F2 on the test set have done?

  • The test set is a fresh sample; choosing on it means the final score was optimized on the very rows used to report it.

  • A threshold is a fitted value. Fitting it on the test rows leaks, just like tuning C on them would.

Show answer

B. A threshold is a fitted value. Fitting it on the test rows leaks, just like tuning C on them would.

Key takeaways

  • Make the evaluation decisions (metric, folds, test set) before training anything, and share one cv object across every candidate.
  • When class weights raise recall but not AP, a tuned threshold gives the same benefit while keeping probabilities meaningful.
  • Check that members disagree before combining them; uncorrelated, similarly strong members are what make an ensemble work.
  • Compare candidates fold by fold, not only by their means.
  • Look at the actual mistakes; they tell you whether the model learned something sensible.

#Extend it

  • Swap the target to another digit (try 1, which is often confused with 7) and see whether the same ensemble still wins.
  • Make the 8s rarer (keep 30) and watch the fold-to-fold spread grow. How many eights per fold do you need before the ranking of models stops changing?
  • Replace soft voting with VotingClassifier(..., weights=[1, 2, 2, 1]) based on the stack's coefficients, and check whether hand-set weights beat the learned stack.
  • Write a cost-based scorer (for example, a miss costs 10 checks) and compare its threshold with the F2 threshold.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Voting Classifier and Stacked generalization (opens in a new tab): parameters such as weights, stack_method, and passthrough, with worked examples.
  • scikit-learn: TunedThresholdClassifierCV reference (opens in a new tab): every option, including store_cv_results for plotting the score at each threshold.
  • scikit-learn: Precision-Recall example (opens in a new tab): how the curve and average precision are computed, and why AP differs from the trapezoidal area under the curve.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compute balanced class weights by hand and prove they equal per-row sample weights.
  • Detect and fix oversampling that happens before the cross-validation split.
  • Choose a decision threshold from out-of-fold probabilities and an explicit cost of each mistake.
  • Explain why hard and soft voting disagree, and why stacking survives a weak member that soft voting doesn't.
  • Judge a popular imbalance trick (undersampling plus bagging) against a plain baseline.

Every exercise below has a trap that shows up in real projects. Write your answer before opening the hint, and run your code before opening the solution. All data is generated or bundled with scikit-learn, so every cell runs offline in Colab.

#Warm-up: what does a coin-flipping model score?

A model gives every row a random score. 2% of the rows are positive. Guess its ROC AUC and its average precision, then check.

ROC AUC sits at 0.5 whatever the imbalance. AP sits at the positive share. So "AP = 0.30" is weak on balanced data and fifteen times better than chance here.

#Exercise 1: Balanced weights by hand

A dataset has 940 negatives and 60 positives. Compute the weights class_weight="balanced" assigns, using the formula n_samples / (n_classes * count_of_class). Then confirm with compute_class_weight, and show that fitting LogisticRegression with class_weight="balanced" gives the same coefficients as passing those weights row by row through sample_weight.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Index the weight array with the label array: weights[y] gives each row its class's weight. Compare coefficients with np.allclose.

Show solution

Each positive weighs 8.333 / 0.532 ≈ 15.7 times as much as a negative, which is exactly 940 / 60. The weights are chosen so that both classes contribute the same total weight (500 each) to the loss.

#Exercise 2: The resampling leak

A teammate oversamples first and cross-validates second, and reports a wonderful AP. Something is wrong with this code:

Explain the problem, then report the AP from the teammate's version, from a correct version that oversamples only the training rows of each fold, and from no oversampling at all.

Need a hint?

Write the loop yourself: for train, val in cv.split(X, y):. Inside it, find the positives among train, repeat them, fit on the enlarged training set, and score predict_proba on X[val], which you never touch.

Show solution

When copies are made before splitting, most validation positives have an identical twin in the training folds, and a 3-nearest-neighbour model finds that twin at distance zero. The "0.94" measures memory, not skill. Done correctly, oversampling actually lowers AP for k-NN here, because the copies pile extra votes onto the exact training points instead of teaching anything new.

#Exercise 3: A threshold from the cost of each mistake

A login-security model flags suspicious sign-ins for an extra verification step. A missed account takeover costs 15 units; an unnecessary verification costs 1. Using out-of-fold probabilities from a scaled logistic regression on make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=8, n_informative=4, weights=[0.95], class_sep=1.0, random_state=21), compute the total cost at thresholds 0.01, 0.02, …, 0.99, plot it, and report the best threshold, its cost, and the cost at 0.5 and at the textbook value 1/16.

Need a hint?

cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba")[:, 1] gives one honest probability per row. For a threshold t, misses are (proba < t) & (y == 1) and false alarms are (proba >= t) & (y == 0).

Show solution

The best threshold is about 0.12, and it costs about 40% less than 0.5. It differs from the textbook 1/16 because that formula assumes perfectly calibrated probabilities, which a logistic regression on this data only roughly gives. Note one subtle point: the minimum was picked on the same out-of-fold predictions it is reported on, so the 837 is a little optimistic. Wrapping the whole procedure in an outer cross-validation, as the Challenge does, fixes that.

#Exercise 4: When hard and soft voting disagree

Fit a hard and a soft VotingClassifier with the same three members: scaled logistic regression, KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=9), and DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0). Use make_classification(n_samples=1500, n_features=8, n_informative=4, flip_y=0.08, class_sep=0.8, random_state=4) with a 60/40 split (random_state=0). Count the test rows where they disagree, print the three members' probabilities for a few of them, and say which voting rule is right more often on those rows.

Need a hint?

After fitting, the soft voter keeps its fitted members in .estimators_. Stack their predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] columns side by side.

Show solution

Look at rows where the tree says 1.00 or 0.00. A depth-5 tree's leaves are often pure, so it is extremely confident, and in a soft vote one extreme number can outweigh two members that lean mildly the other way. Hard voting ignores confidence and counts heads. On this data hard voting wins slightly on the rows where they disagree, which shows that soft voting is only better when every member's probabilities are reasonably calibrated.

#Exercise 5: One weak member sinks the vote

Compare, with 5-fold AP on make_classification(n_samples=2500, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.92], class_sep=1.0, random_state=8): a RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0) alone, GaussianNB alone, a depth-1 tree alone, a soft vote of all three, and a stack of all three with a logistic-regression final estimator. Then print the stack's final coefficients.

Need a hint?

Use one StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) for every candidate. After fitting the stack on all the data, read final_estimator_.coef_.

Show solution

Soft voting gives every member an equal say, so two weak members drag the forest's AP down by almost 0.09. The stack learns how much to trust each member from out-of-fold predictions: it gives the forest a large weight, the Bayes model a small one, and the stump a slightly negative one, and ends up matching the forest. If you must vote, pass weights= or leave weak members out.

#Exercise 6: Undersampling plus bagging, tested honestly

A popular recipe for rare classes: train many trees, each on all the positives plus an equally sized random sample of negatives, then average their probabilities. On make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.98], class_sep=1.0, random_state=2) with a stratified 60/40 split, compare the test AP of 25 such balanced trees against one tree on all the training data and a RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100) on all the training data.

Need a hint?

Find the indices of positives and negatives in y_train. In each of 25 rounds, use rng.choice(neg, size=len(pos), replace=False), fit a fresh DecisionTreeClassifier, and keep its predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]. Average the 25 columns.

Show solution

The balanced bag roughly doubles a single tree's AP, but the forest trained on every row doubles it again. Each balanced tree saw only 184 rows and threw away 98% of the negatives, and with negatives this varied, that lost information matters. Undersampling shines when the data is too big to train on comfortably, not as a default.

#Challenge: Compare strategies on a real cost, with no optimism

Use load_diabetes, with "high progression" (target > 250, about 15% of patients) as the positive class, and imagine flagging patients for an earlier follow-up, where a missed high-progression patient costs 5 and an unnecessary appointment costs 1. Write code that, for three strategies (plain logistic regression, class_weight="balanced" logistic regression, and a soft vote of logistic regression with 15-nearest-neighbours), reports with one outer 5-fold split: cross-validated AP, the average cost per fold at the 0.5 default, and the average cost per fold when the threshold is tuned inside each outer training fold with TunedThresholdClassifierCV.

Need a hint?

TunedThresholdClassifierCV is itself an estimator, so you can pass it to cross_val_score as the model. That gives nested evaluation: the threshold is chosen on each outer training fold and scored on the outer validation fold. Make your scorer return the negative cost.

Show solution

Three things stand out. All three strategies rank about equally well (AP 0.55 to 0.57), so the ensemble buys nothing here. Tuning the threshold rescues the plain model, cutting its cost by about a third. And the balanced model at plain 0.5 is already about as good as any tuned threshold. That is not luck: balancing makes the classes' total weights equal, which acts like a miss costing 377/65 ≈ 5.8 times a false alarm, very close to the 5 we chose. With the cost known, a tuned threshold gets there without needing that coincidence.

What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between bagging (random forests) and boosting in terms of bias and variance.
  • Trace how gradient boosting improves a prediction by fitting the residuals of the previous round.
  • Use HistGradientBoostingClassifier with early stopping, and say when to prefer it over a random forest.
  • Explain why impurity-based feature_importances_ can rank a meaningless column highly, and check importance with permutation_importance.
  • Tell target leakage apart from train-test contamination, and show contamination inflating a score.

A subscription company's churn model scores ROC AUC 0.99 in cross-validation. Its most important feature is days_since_last_login. Then someone notices that the column was computed on the day the data was exported, weeks after the customers in the table had already cancelled, and of course people who cancelled stopped logging in. The model hasn't learned to predict churn. It has learned to read the answer from a column that was written after the fact.

Random forests and gradient boosting are the two strongest general-purpose models for tables, and they are also the two that find a leaked column fastest. This module compares them properly, then teaches you to spot the leak before it wins the comparison for you.

#Two ways to build a team of trees

A single deep decision tree fits its training data closely, so a slightly different training set gives a noticeably different tree. That sensitivity is variance. A shallow tree is stable but too simple to follow the real pattern. That systematic miss is bias. The two big ensembles attack different halves of the problem.

  • Bagging (random forests) trains hundreds of deep trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows and with a random subset of features at each split, then averages them. Averaging many noisy but different trees cancels much of their variance while keeping their low bias.
  • Boosting trains shallow trees one after another, each fitted to the errors the ensemble is still making. Every round chips away at the bias. Because the trees stay small, variance grows slowly, but it does grow if you keep adding rounds.

The experiment below draws 25 different training sets of 60 noisy points from the same curve, fits each model to every set, and plots all 25 fitted lines. Spread between the lines is variance; distance between their average and the true curve is bias.

The deep tree has almost no bias and by far the most variance. The forest keeps the deep tree's low bias and halves its variance just by averaging. Boosting is built from the same depth-2 trees as the first panel, yet adding 100 of them in sequence cuts that panel's bias by more than ten times while adding very little variance.

#Boosting, one correction at a time

Here is gradient boosting for squared error with nothing hidden. Start by predicting the mean. Each round, compute the residuals (truth minus prediction), fit a one-split tree to them, and move every prediction a fraction of the way (the learning rate) toward that tree's output. A real booster searches for the best split each round; here the splits are given so the trace stays short.

The biggest residual goes from 4.0 to 1.91 in three rounds. With a learning rate of 0.5 each tree only takes half a step, so the ensemble needs more rounds but is less likely to chase noise. That trade (smaller rate, more rounds) is the main dial on any booster.

scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier and HistGradientBoostingRegressor first sort each feature's values into at most 255 bins, which makes split search fast on large tables. They also handle missing values without imputation and can treat pandas category columns as categories directly. Because extra rounds can eventually overfit, they offer early stopping: hold out a slice of the training data, track the loss on it, and stop when it hasn't improved for n_iter_no_change rounds. It switches on by itself above 10,000 rows; on smaller data, set early_stopping=True.

The scores are stored as negative losses (higher is better), which is why the code flips their sign. With a high learning rate of 0.3 the held-out loss stops improving after about 16 rounds; the model ran 20 more to be sure, then stopped. Without early stopping it would have run all 500.

Random forest Histogram gradient boosting
Trees deep, independent, averaged shallow, sequential, summed
Mainly reduces variance bias
More trees never hurts accuracy, only time can overfit; use early stopping
Key knobs max_features, min_samples_leaf learning_rate, max_iter, max_leaf_nodes
Large tables slower fast, thanks to binning
Missing values, categories missing values yes; categories need encoding both handled natively

#The serial-number trap in feature importance

Tree ensembles offer a tempting shortcut, feature_importances_, which adds up how much each feature reduced impurity across all splits. It has two flaws: it is computed on the training data, and features with many distinct values offer many more split points to overfit with. To see this, take a machine-fault dataset with three real sensors, one real yes/no feature (night_shift), and two columns of pure noise: a unique serial_number and a coin_flip.

Impurity importance puts serial_number fourth, about twice as important as night_shift, which genuinely drives faults. Permutation importance asks a better question: if I shuffle this column in the test set, breaking its link with the target, how much does the test score drop? Shuffling the serial number changes nothing (−0.001, well inside its own standard deviation), while shuffling night_shift costs 0.11 of AUC, making it the second most useful feature. HistGradientBoosting models don't even offer feature_importances_, so permutation importance is the tool for both families. Module 7 looks at its own pitfall, correlated features.

#Leakage comes in two flavours

Target leakage means a feature carries information that won't exist when the model is used, usually because it was recorded after, or because of, the outcome. The churn column in the opening story is one. So is "antibiotics prescribed" when predicting infection, or "final invoice amount" when predicting whether an order ships. No validation scheme catches it, because the leak is real in every row; only asking "when is this value known?" does.

Train-test contamination means information from the evaluation rows reaches training. Fitting a scaler or feature selector on all rows before cross-validation is the version pipelines prevent. The sneakier version is the same entity (a patient, a customer, a machine) appearing in several rows that land on both sides of a split. The model learns to recognize the entity rather than the pattern. Here are 120 people with 8 recordings each, where the label belongs to the person:

Splitting by row gives 0.98; keeping each person's recordings in one fold gives about 0.60, which is what the model will really do for a new person. That is a bigger swing than any difference between model families you'll see in this module. The fixes are the splitters from Module 3: StratifiedGroupKFold for repeated entities, and TimeSeriesSplit for time-ordered data, where shuffling lets the model train on the future to predict the past. The flexible models in this module are the ones best at exploiting the leak, so the split matters even more here.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic mistakes with tree ensembles

  1. Reading feature_importances_ as truth. It is measured on training data and favours many-valued columns. Use permutation_importance on held-out data.
  2. Comparing a tuned booster with a default forest. Give both families a comparable tuning budget on the same folds, or the comparison says more about effort than about models.
  3. Celebrating a near-perfect score. An AUC of 0.99 on a messy real-world problem is more often a leak than a breakthrough. Check the top feature and ask when its value becomes known.
  4. Splitting rows when the data has repeated entities. If one customer or patient can appear twice, split by group.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your random forest overfits less as you add trees, but your gradient boosting model starts to get worse after 300 rounds. Why the difference?

  • It's the other way around: forest trees are usually deep, and boosting trees are shallow.

  • That's why boosters need early stopping or a tuned max_iter, while a forest just needs "enough" trees.

  • The 255 limit is on the number of bins per feature, not on the number of rounds.

Show answer

B. That's why boosters need early stopping or a tuned max_iter, while a forest just needs "enough" trees.

2A random forest's feature_importances_ ranks customer_id third. What should you do first?

  • The forest used it to memorize training rows; that rarely transfers to new customers.

  • If shuffling the column on test rows doesn't hurt, its impurity importance came from memorization.

  • Hiding the symptom doesn't remove the problem.

Show answer

B. If shuffling the column on test rows doesn't hurt, its impurity importance came from memorization.

3Which of these is target leakage rather than train-test contamination?

  • That lets validation rows influence training: contamination, and a pipeline fixes it.

  • Collection calls happen because of default, so the value isn't available when the loan decision is made.

  • That's contamination through a shared entity; group splitting fixes it.

Show answer

B. Collection calls happen because of default, so the value isn't available when the loan decision is made.

Key takeaways

  • Random forests average deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees in sequence to cut bias.
  • Boosting's learning rate and number of rounds trade against each other; early stopping picks the number of rounds from held-out data.
  • Impurity-based importances are biased toward many-valued features and measured on training data. Use permutation importance on held-out data.
  • Target leakage is a feature that knows the future; contamination is evaluation rows reaching training. Ask "when is this value known?" for the first, and split by group or time for the second.

  • scikit-learn: Permutation importance vs. MDI (opens in a new tab): the official example of a random column fooling impurity importance.
  • scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and recommended practices (opens in a new tab): data leakage during preprocessing and how pipelines prevent it.

What you'll learn

  • Compare RandomForestClassifier and HistGradientBoostingClassifier on identical folds, each with suitable preprocessing.
  • Use permutation importance and single-feature scores to find a column that leaks the target.
  • Detect repeated entities and switch to StratifiedGroupKFold so no customer is split across folds.
  • Measure how much each leak inflated the score, and report which model wins once both are fixed.

A streaming service hands you an export: one row per customer per month for the last quarter, and a column saying whether that customer cancelled by the end of the quarter. The question from the product team is simple: "Should we use a random forest or gradient boosting to predict cancellations?" You'll answer it three times. The first two answers will be wrong, and finding out why is the point.

Here is the finished picture, so you know where the steps lead.

#Step 1: Load the export and read its data dictionary

The code below builds a realistic stand-in for the export. In a real project this would be pd.read_csv(...); generating it lets everyone get identical numbers. The first two lines cap boosting at one CPU thread, which the note after this step explains.

📝 Note

HistGradientBoosting runs on every CPU core by default. That is fast on your own machine, but on a busy shared computer, or inside a parallel grid search where every worker also grabs every core, the threads fight and a two-second fit can take a minute. The scikit-learn docs call this oversubscription. threadpool_limits caps the threads; in Colab you can delete those lines without harm.

The data team's dictionary for the columns, exactly as they wrote it:

Column Meaning
plan, contract, region, monthly_fee account details
tenure_months months since sign-up, at that monthly snapshot
logins_30d, support_tickets_30d, payment_failures activity in the 30 days before the snapshot
days_since_last_login days between the last login and the date this file was exported
cancelled 1 if the customer cancelled by the end of the quarter

Read the dictionary again before moving on. One row in it should worry you.

#Step 2: Race 1, with every column

The forest needs the three text columns one-hot encoded. Boosting can use them directly because they have pandas category dtype and categorical_features="from_dtype" is the default. A helper runs both models on the same folds so we can reuse it for every race.

Both models score about 0.99. Cancellation is a hard problem, driven by things nobody records, like how much someone actually enjoys the service. A near-perfect score on a hard problem is a reason to investigate, not to celebrate.

#Step 3: Interrogate the winner

Ask the model what it relies on. We hold out a quarter of the customers (with GroupShuffleSplit, so no customer is on both sides), fit boosting on the rest, and shuffle one column at a time on the held-out rows.

Shuffling days_since_last_login wipes out more than 0.35 of AUC; the next most important column costs 0.016. On its own, with no model at all, that column separates cancellers from stayers with an AUC around 0.97.

Now go back to the dictionary: days between the last login and the date this file was exported. The export happened after the quarter ended. Customers who cancelled stopped logging in, so by export day they had been away for weeks. The column is a consequence of the outcome. On the day you'd actually use the model, at a monthly snapshot before anyone has cancelled, this value doesn't exist in this form. That is target leakage, and the only fix is to drop the column (or rebuild it from data stamped before the snapshot).

#Step 4: Race 2, with the leak removed

About 0.89 to 0.90, with boosting ahead. These look like believable numbers for a cancellation model, and this is where most notebooks stop. But look at the first line Step 1 printed: 2,390 rows and only 800 customers.

Every customer has 2 to 4 rows, all sharing one label. And monthly_fee, thanks to personal discounts, is close to a fingerprint: 467 distinct values for 800 customers, and never more than one per customer. With rows shuffled into folds, most validation rows have a sibling row from the same customer in training, with the same fee and the same answer. The models can score well by recognizing customers instead of predicting behaviour. That is train-test contamination through a repeated entity, the same trap as the repeat patients in Module 3, now hiding behind a leak you already fixed.

#Step 5: Race 3, with customers kept together

StratifiedGroupKFold keeps every customer's rows in a single fold while balancing the cancelled share across folds.

Both scores fall again, and the order flips: the forest is now ahead by about 0.02, and it wins in four of the five folds. Boosting's lead in Race 2 came from memorizing customers slightly better, not from predicting new ones better.

#Step 6: See how much of each score was real

The leak was worth about 0.10 of AUC and the contamination another 0.06 to 0.09. Together they were larger than any difference between the two model families, which is the general lesson: fix the evaluation first, then compare models.

#The finished evaluation

Here is the honest comparison as one reusable function. It refuses to run if you pass it a column on a "known leaks" list, and it always groups by customer.

With a different fold seed the forest still leads, by a little less (about 0.01). Rerunning with new seeds is a cheap check that a result isn't an accident of one particular split, and here it says the forest's lead is real but small.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did Step 3 hold out data with GroupShuffleSplit instead of a plain train_test_split?

  • It accepts any held-out set; the grouping is about what the importances mean.

  • If held-out rows had siblings in training, columns that fingerprint customers (like monthly_fee) would look more useful than they are.

  • Splitting rows never removes columns; both sets always have every column.

Show answer

B. If held-out rows had siblings in training, columns that fingerprint customers (like monthly_fee) would look more useful than they are.

2Race 2's scores (about 0.89 to 0.90) looked believable. What was the clue that they were still inflated?

  • Repeated entities with a shared label let a model score by recognition, so row-shuffled folds overstate performance on new customers.

  • Either model winning is plausible; the problem was in how the folds were built.

  • The spread was ordinary; the issue was that validation rows weren't truly new.

Show answer

A. Repeated entities with a shared label let a model score by recognition, so row-shuffled folds overstate performance on new customers.

3After all fixes the forest leads by about 0.02. What should you do before telling the product team "use the forest"?

  • Five folds is a small sample, and boosting hasn't been tuned at all.

  • A 0.02 gap between untuned defaults can easily reverse after tuning, so the comparison should hold up under both before it drives a decision.

  • Stable but wrong numbers are worse than noisy honest ones.

Show answer

B. A 0.02 gap between untuned defaults can easily reverse after tuning, so the comparison should hold up under both before it drives a decision.

Key takeaways

  • A near-perfect score on a hard problem is a prompt to investigate; check the top permutation-importance feature and each column's solo AUC.
  • For every column, ask when its value becomes known. Anything recorded after the moment of prediction is target leakage.
  • Count rows per entity. If customers, patients, or devices repeat, split with GroupKFold or StratifiedGroupKFold.
  • Leakage can change which model wins, not just how good both look. Fix the evaluation before comparing models.

#Extend it

  • Tune both models with RandomizedSearchCV (about 20 candidates each) inside the grouped folds and see whether boosting catches up.
  • Rebuild days_since_last_login the honest way: days between the last login and the snapshot date. Generate it from the snapshot rows and test whether it still helps.
  • Replace ROC AUC with average precision and check whether the ranking of the two models changes.
  • Add a month column to the features. Does it leak anything? Ask when its value is known.

#Further reading

  • Kapoor and Narayanan: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science (opens in a new tab): a taxonomy of eight types of leakage, plus a running list of studies that found errors affecting more than 600 published papers across 30 fields.
  • scikit-learn: Cross-validation iterators for grouped data (opens in a new tab): GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold, and friends, with diagrams of how each splits.
  • scikit-learn: Parallelism and resource management (opens in a new tab): why thread oversubscription happens and how to control it.

What you'll learn

  • Use out-of-bag scores to decide how many trees a random forest needs.
  • Trade learning rate against boosting rounds with early stopping.
  • Diagnose bias and variance from training and validation scores.
  • Show how correlated features split permutation importance, and measure them jointly.
  • Catch leakage from target encoding and from shuffled time-ordered data, and fix both.

These exercises go from tuning the two ensembles to catching leaks that don't look like leaks. Boosting cells start by capping OpenMP threads, as in the Build-along, so they stay fast on a shared machine; in Colab you can drop those lines.

#Warm-up: safe, target leak, or contamination?

For each situation, decide before opening the solution.

  1. Predicting next month's loan default from missed_payments_last_6_months, measured at the start of the month.
  2. Predicting customer churn from account_closed_reason.
  3. Scaling every image by the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset, then cross-validating.
  4. Five X-rays per patient, with rows shuffled into folds.
  5. Predicting a diagnosis from treatment_given.
Show solution
  1. Safe. It is known before the outcome.
  2. Target leak. The reason only exists after the account has closed.
  3. Contamination. Validation images influenced the scaling. Usually small, but a pipeline removes it for free.
  4. Contamination. The model can recognize patients; split with GroupKFold.
  5. Target leak. Treatment is chosen because of the diagnosis.

#Exercise 1: How many trees does a forest need?

Each tree in a random forest skips about a third of the rows in its bootstrap sample. Scoring every row using only the trees that didn't see it gives the out-of-bag (OOB) score, a free validation estimate. On load_digits, grow one forest with warm_start=True from 10 to 200 trees and print the OOB accuracy at 10, 25, 50, 100, and 200 trees. Where does adding trees stop paying off?

Need a hint?

Create RandomForestClassifier(oob_score=True, warm_start=True, random_state=0), then in a loop call set_params(n_estimators=n) and fit again. With warm_start, each fit only adds the new trees. Expect a warning at 10 trees: some rows haven't been left out by any tree yet.

Show solution

Accuracy climbs fast to 100 trees and then creeps up by a fraction of a percent. More trees never make a forest worse; they just cost time. Pick the point where the curve flattens for your budget.

#Exercise 2: Learning rate against rounds

On make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=20, n_informative=8, flip_y=0.05, random_state=0), fit HistGradientBoostingClassifier with early stopping (max_iter=1000, validation_fraction=0.2, n_iter_no_change=15) at learning rates 0.3, 0.1, and 0.03. Report the number of rounds used (n_iter_) and the best held-out log loss for each.

Need a hint?

The held-out scores are in validation_score_, stored as negative loss. The best loss is -validation_score_.max().

Show solution

Cutting the rate by 10 multiplies the rounds by about 6 and buys a slightly better loss. That is the usual pattern: a small learning rate with early stopping is a safe default, and the price is training time.

#Exercise 3: Bias or variance?

Using cross_validate(..., return_train_score=True) with ROC AUC on make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=20, n_informative=8, flip_y=0.05, random_state=1), compare a depth-2 decision tree, an unlimited decision tree, a random forest, and histogram gradient boosting. For each, say whether its main problem is bias, variance, or neither.

Need a hint?

High bias: training and validation scores are both mediocre and close together. High variance: training is near perfect but validation is much lower.

Show solution

The depth-2 tree has bias: about 0.8 on both. The deep tree has variance: perfect on training, 0.85 on validation. The forest and boosting also score near 1.0 on training, yet both reach about 0.97 on validation. A perfect training score is normal for these ensembles; what matters is the validation score and its gap to other models, not the gap to training.

#Exercise 4: A duplicated feature hides its own importance

On load_diabetes(as_frame=True) with a 70/30 split (random_state=0), fit RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=0) and print the top permutation importances on the test set. Then add bmi_copy (bmi plus tiny noise), refit, and print them again. Finally, measure the drop in test R² when you shuffle bmi and bmi_copy together, with the same permutation.

Need a hint?

For the joint shuffle, draw one permutation perm and assign X_shuffled[["bmi", "bmi_copy"]] = X_test[["bmi", "bmi_copy"]].values[perm]. Compare model.score before and after, averaged over a few permutations.

Show solution

Alone, bmi is the second most important feature (0.157). With a near-identical copy, the credit splits unevenly: bmi_copy keeps about a third of it and bmi drops out of the top four, because shuffling one twin leaves the other to carry the information. Shuffled together, they cost 0.150, about what bmi was worth alone. Real data is full of near-twins (the diabetes features s1 and s2 correlate at about 0.9), so group strongly correlated features and permute each group together.

#Exercise 5: The target-encoding leak

Target encoding replaces each category with the average target for that category. A teammate encodes a 400-value zip_code column using all the rows, then cross-validates a logistic regression on it. The target below is pure noise, so the honest AUC is 0.5. Reproduce their result, then fix it with scikit-learn's TargetEncoder inside a pipeline.

Need a hint?

TargetEncoder uses internal cross-fitting in fit_transform: each row is encoded with statistics from other folds, so a row never sees its own label. Put it in a make_column_transformer for the zip_code column with remainder="passthrough".

Show solution

With only 5 rows per zip code, each row's own label makes up a fifth of its encoding, so the encoded value partly is the answer. The leaky version scores about 0.76 on noise. Inside the pipeline, encodings are learned on training folds only and cross-fitted within them, and the score falls to 0.5, which is the truth.

#Exercise 6: Shuffled time series

A shop's daily demand depends on temperature, promotions, and a slowly wandering level of popularity. Generate two years of it as below, then estimate a random forest's mean absolute error with shuffled KFold and with TimeSeriesSplit. Which number would you put in a report, and why are they so different?

Need a hint?

TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5) always trains on earlier days and tests on the block that follows. Use scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error" and flip the sign.

Show solution

Report the TimeSeriesSplit number, about 26. With shuffled folds, every test day has training days on both sides of it, and the day column lets the forest look up the popularity level of its neighbours: interpolation, which is easy. In real use the model must extrapolate into the future, where popularity has drifted, and the error is more than four times larger.

#Challenge: Write a leak scanner

Write leak_scan(df, target, group_col=None) that prints three warnings: any single column whose ROC AUC against the target is above 0.9 (or below 0.1), whether any group appears in more than one row, and how many rows are exact duplicates of another row once the target is removed. Test it on this planted dataset, which hides one of each problem.

Need a hint?

For a numeric column, roc_auc_score(df[target], df[col]) works directly; use max(auc, 1 - auc) so a column that predicts the opposite way is caught too. Skipping text columns is fine for a first version. df.drop(columns=target).duplicated().sum() counts duplicate rows.

Show solution

All three warnings fire. days_in_hospital is a consequence of being sick, most of the 150 patients appear more than once, and the re-imported rows are exact copies. A scanner like this won't find every leak, but it costs a second and catches the loud ones before they win a model comparison for you.
