What you'll learn

  • Draw a reliability diagram with CalibrationDisplay and explain what the Brier score and log loss measure.
  • Recalibrate a classifier with CalibratedClassifierCV, choosing between sigmoid and isotonic.
  • Explain a model's behaviour with permutation_importance, partial dependence, and ICE curves, and know what each can't tell you.
  • Compute errors per subgroup, attach uncertainty to each, and compare against a per-slice baseline.

A weather app says "70% chance of rain" on 100 different days. If it rained on about 70 of them, the forecasts were calibrated. If it rained on 95, the app was too timid; on 40, too confident. Ranking metrics like ROC AUC can't see the difference. They only check that rainy days got higher numbers than dry ones.

That matters the moment someone uses the number itself: to compute an expected cost, to set a threshold from costs as in Module 5, or to tell a person "your risk is 30%". So before recommending a model, check three more things: whether its probabilities mean what they say, whether its reasoning makes sense, and where its mistakes concentrate.

#Same ranking, different probabilities

Here are three classifiers on the same data. Two of them rank the test rows almost identically well.

Each point groups the test rows by predicted probability (0 to 0.1, 0.1 to 0.2, and so on) and plots the average prediction against the share that really were positive. Boosting stays close to the diagonal. The forest has the same ROC AUC, but its curve is an S: when it says 0.25 the true rate is about 0.1, and when it says 0.75 it is about 0.9. Averaging hundreds of trees pulls predictions toward the middle, because it is rare for every tree to agree on an extreme. Naive Bayes assumes the features are independent, so on data with redundant features it double-counts evidence and its probabilities swing badly.

Two scores summarize calibration and sharpness together:

  • Brier score: the mean of (p − y)². Zero is perfect; always predicting 0.5 on balanced data scores 0.25.
  • Log loss: the mean of −log(probability given to what actually happened). It punishes confident mistakes very hard: a 0.99 on a row that turns out negative costs 4.6, while a 0.6 costs 0.9.

Both are proper scoring rules: a model gets its best expected score by reporting its true beliefs, so neither can be gamed by shading probabilities up or down.

#Recalibrate with CalibratedClassifierCV

Calibration fits a small one-input model that maps a classifier's raw scores to better probabilities. scikit-learn offers two main mappings:

  • method="sigmoid" (Platt scaling) fits a logistic curve. It has two parameters, so it works on small data but can only fix S-shaped distortions.
  • method="isotonic" fits any non-decreasing step function. It can fix any monotonic distortion but needs more data, roughly a thousand rows or more, or it overfits.

The mapping must be learned on predictions for rows the classifier didn't train on. CalibratedClassifierCV(model, cv=5) handles that: on each fold it trains the model on four fifths of the data, fits the calibrator on the remaining fifth, and at prediction time averages the five calibrated pairs.

The calibrated forest now matches boosting on Brier score and log loss, with the same ROC AUC: calibration repaired the probabilities without touching the ranking. Naive Bayes improves too, and isotonic beats sigmoid because its distortion isn't a simple S. Calibration can't add ranking skill, though; naive Bayes still ranks worst.

📝 Note

To calibrate a model you have already trained, wrap it in FrozenEstimator (in sklearn.frozen, available since scikit-learn 1.6) and fit CalibratedClassifierCV on a separate calibration set. Older tutorials use cv="prefit", which newer versions have removed. And remember Module 5: a model trained with class_weight="balanced" is miscalibrated on purpose, so calibrate it before using its probabilities.

#What the model relies on: permutation importance

The diabetes dataset predicts a disease-progression score one year after 10 baseline measurements. Loading it with scaled=False keeps real units (age in years, BMI, blood pressure). We'll fit a small boosted model and ask which features its test-set accuracy depends on.

With scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error", the importance is in the target's own units: shuffling s5 (a blood serum measurement) makes predictions worse by about 10 points on average. Two cautions from Module 6 still apply. Compute it on held-out data, and remember that correlated features share credit, so a low score can mean "redundant" rather than "useless". Importance also says how much the model uses a feature, never which direction it pushes.

#Which direction: partial dependence and ICE curves

A partial dependence curve answers: if every row had BMI = 25, what would the average prediction be? Then 26, 27, and so on. Here is the computation by hand for a made-up model and three patients.

Each inner value, model(value, age) for one patient, is a point on that patient's ICE (individual conditional expectation) curve. The partial dependence curve is their average. At BMI 40 the three ICE values differ (270, 330, 300) because the model has an age interaction there, which the average alone would hide. PartialDependenceDisplay with kind="both" draws both at once.

Predicted progression climbs with both features, from about 130 to 215 across the BMI range, with the biggest jumps near BMI 27 and 33 and near s5 = 4.9. The curves are staircases because a boosted model is a sum of trees, and every tree is a step function. The ICE lines mostly run parallel at different heights, so the model shifts every patient by a similar amount. If they crossed or fanned out, the average would be hiding an interaction. One limit: partial dependence pretends you can change one feature while holding the others fixed. When features are strongly correlated, that creates patients who could never exist, and the curve over those regions is guesswork.

#Where it fails: errors by slice

An average error hides how it is distributed. Slice-based error analysis computes the error separately for meaningful subgroups. Three rules make it trustworthy: use out-of-fold predictions for every row, attach an uncertainty interval to each slice, and compare each slice with a baseline on the same slice, since some groups are simply harder to predict.

On raw error, the two higher-BMI slices look alike (about 54 and 50) and much worse than BMI under 25. The baseline column changes the story. Outcomes in the BMI 30+ group vary far more (the baseline is off by 81 points there), so the model is actually removing a large share of the error, with a skill of 0.38. The slice where the model helps least is BMI 25 to 30, with a skill of only 0.16. That is the one worth investigating. Also check the intervals: with 95 patients in the BMI 30+ slice, its interval is 15 points wide, so a gap of a few points between slices is noise.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic mistakes

  1. Calibrating on the training data. The model's in-sample predictions are overconfident, so the calibrator learns the wrong mapping. Use CalibratedClassifierCV with cv, or a separate calibration set.
  2. Using isotonic calibration on a few hundred rows. It overfits into a jagged staircase. Use sigmoid on small data.
  3. Reading a partial dependence plot as cause and effect. It shows what the model does when you change an input, not what would happen to a patient. And with correlated features it extrapolates into impossible combinations.
  4. Declaring the worst slice a problem without an interval or a baseline. The worst of many small slices always looks bad by chance, and some groups are simply harder.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Two models have the same ROC AUC. Model A's Brier score is 0.036 and model B's is 0.041. What can you conclude?

  • Equal ROC AUC means they rank about equally well; the Brier gap comes from the probabilities themselves.

  • With ranking equal, the Brier difference reflects calibration, which is what a cost-based threshold or a risk estimate relies on.

  • Brier score alone doesn't diagnose overfitting; compare train and validation scores for that.

Show answer

B. With ranking equal, the Brier difference reflects calibration, which is what a cost-based threshold or a risk estimate relies on.

2You have 300 labelled rows to calibrate an SVM's scores. Which method is the safer choice?

  • Two parameters can't overfit much, which matters with only 300 rows.

  • Isotonic regression can fit any staircase, so with 300 rows it tends to memorize noise.

  • SVM decision values aren't probabilities at all; they need a mapping.

Show answer

A. Two parameters can't overfit much, which matters with only 300 rows.

3A partial dependence curve for income is flat, but the ICE lines form an X: half rise, half fall. What does that mean?

  • The individual lines move a lot; they just cancel out on average.

  • The average hides opposite effects, which is exactly what ICE curves exist to reveal.

  • ICE curves describe how predictions change with an input, not whether probabilities match outcome rates.

Show answer

B. The average hides opposite effects, which is exactly what ICE curves exist to reveal.

4The error rate for one region is 9% versus 6% overall, measured on 40 rows. What should you check first?

  • That might come later, but first you need to know whether the gap is real.

  • With 40 rows a 3-point gap can be chance, and the region might be harder for any model.

Show answer

B. With 40 rows a 3-point gap can be chance, and the region might be harder for any model.

Key takeaways

  • ROC AUC measures ranking; reliability diagrams, Brier score, and log loss measure whether probabilities can be taken at face value.
  • CalibratedClassifierCV fixes probabilities without changing the ranking. Prefer sigmoid on small data and isotonic on large data, and always calibrate on rows the model didn't train on.
  • Permutation importance says how much a model uses a feature; partial dependence and ICE curves show in which direction, and whether the effect differs between rows.
  • Slice errors need out-of-fold predictions, intervals, and a per-slice baseline before they mean anything.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Probability calibration (opens in a new tab): calibration curves, the sigmoid and isotonic methods, and the cross-validation scheme behind CalibratedClassifierCV.
  • scikit-learn: Partial dependence and ICE plots (opens in a new tab): how both are computed, the fast recursion method for tree models, and their assumptions.
  • Christoph Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning (opens in a new tab): free online book with clear chapters on permutation importance, PDP, and ICE, including their failure modes.

What you'll learn

  • Show that a ROC AUC tie can hide differences that change a decision.
  • Diagnose and repair a class-weighted model's probabilities with CalibratedClassifierCV.

A school library lends books, DVDs, and laptops, and about 38% of loans come back late. The librarians want a model that estimates the chance each new loan will be late, so they can send a friendly reminder to the riskiest third. A previous student project left two candidate models: a logistic regression trained with class_weight="balanced" and a gradient-boosted model. Their cross-validated ROC AUCs differ by about 0.01. Which should the library use?

By the end you'll have a short evidence table like this one, with the numbers filled in by your own run:

Question Logistic (balanced) Boosting
Ranks loans well overall? step 2 step 2
Probabilities trustworthy? step 3 step 3
Relies on sensible features? step 4 step 4
Works for every item type? step 5 step 5

#Step 1: Load the loans and seal a test set

As in earlier modules, the data is generated so everyone gets the same numbers; the columns are what a library system could export at checkout time. The thread cap at the top is the same one from Module 6.

#Step 2: Confirm the tie

Both models go into the same StratifiedKFold. We keep their out-of-fold probabilities, because every later step reuses them.

0.718 against 0.728. With 3,750 training loans that gap is about the size of the noise, so on ranking alone this is a tie. If we stopped here we'd pick by coin flip or by habit.

#Step 3: Check whether the probabilities mean what they say

The library plans to use the probabilities directly ("remind anyone above 40%"), so calibration matters.

The balanced logistic regression says the average loan has a 48% chance of being late, when the real share is 38%. That's the price of class_weight="balanced" from Module 5: it pushed every score toward the rare class. Under a "remind above 40%" rule it would flag far more loans than intended. Sigmoid recalibration fixes the scale, bringing its Brier score level with boosting's, and leaves its ROC AUC exactly where it was. So calibration doesn't break the tie either; it just removes one reason to reject the logistic model.

#Step 4: Compare what the models rely on

Permutation importance needs a fitted model and rows it didn't see, so we carve a validation set out of the training data.

Both use the same five features, but boosting leans on distance_km and item_type noticeably more, and the logistic model barely uses item_type at all. Importance can't say why. Partial dependence can, especially if we compute it separately for laptops and for everything else.

Here is the difference. Boosting has learned two separate stories: for books and DVDs, distance barely matters until a long trip (around 9 km here), but for laptops the risk starts low and climbs fast with distance, perhaps because a laptop is awkward to carry back from far away. The boosting curves are jagged because each is an average over only a few hundred validation loans. The logistic model has one coefficient for distance shared by every item type, so its two curves have the same shape, just shifted. It averages the two stories, which is a little wrong for books and very wrong for laptops.

#Step 5: Slice the errors by item type and borrower

If the logistic model misunderstands laptops, its errors should pile up there. We compute ROC AUC per slice from the out-of-fold probabilities, with a bootstrap interval so small slices don't fool us.

For books, DVDs, and every borrower group the two models are within about 0.03 of each other, with overlapping intervals. Laptops are different: boosting ranks them at about 0.79 and the logistic model at about 0.66, and the intervals don't overlap. That is a real failure, invisible in the overall score because laptops are only one loan in ten. If the library ever lends more laptops, the logistic model will get worse while its headline number stays the same.

#Step 6: Decide, then confirm once on the test set

The evidence points to boosting: same overall ranking, probabilities that are already calibrated, and it understands the laptop pattern. Now we fit both finalists on all the training data and score the sealed test set once, overall and on laptops.

The test set agrees with the cross-validated evidence: overall the two are nearly identical, and boosting is still ahead on laptops (about 0.76 against 0.71). With only 121 test laptops that test gap alone would be weak evidence, but it points the same way as the larger cross-validated one. Here is the evidence table, filled in.

Question Logistic (balanced) Boosting
Ranks loans well overall? yes, about 0.72 yes, about 0.73
Probabilities trustworthy? no, until recalibrated yes
Relies on sensible features? one distance effect for every item separate distance effects per item type
Works for every item type? weak on laptops (about 0.66) yes (about 0.79 on laptops)

The recommendation writes itself: use boosting, and keep monitoring the laptop slice, because it has the fewest loans and the widest intervals.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1After recalibration, the logistic model's Brier score matched boosting's. Why didn't that settle the choice?

  • Sigmoid recalibration is monotonic, so the AUC stayed exactly the same.

  • Overall Brier and AUC can tie while one slice is badly served; only the slice analysis revealed it.

  • Brier score applies to any probability; it's how we saw the weighted model was off in the first place.

Show answer

B. Overall Brier and AUC can tie while one slice is badly served; only the slice analysis revealed it.

2Why did Step 4 compute partial dependence separately for laptops and for other items instead of once for all loans?

  • Laptops are 10% of loans, so their steep curve would barely bend the average.

  • It handles them; splitting the data was a choice to expose an interaction.

  • Computing twice is slower; the point was to see two stories instead of one.

Show answer

A. Laptops are 10% of loans, so their steep curve would barely bend the average.

3The laptop slice has about 360 loans in training. Why attach bootstrap intervals to its AUC?

  • It doesn't change the estimate; it shows how much the estimate could move with a different sample.

  • With a few hundred rows, AUC can move by several hundredths by chance; non-overlapping intervals make the gap believable.

Show answer

B. With a few hundred rows, AUC can move by several hundredths by chance; non-overlapping intervals make the gap believable.

Key takeaways

  • A tie on ROC AUC is where evaluation starts, not where it ends.
  • Class-weighted models need recalibration before their probabilities can drive a threshold.
  • Permutation importance tells you what a model uses; partial dependence per subgroup shows interactions a single curve hides.
  • Slice the out-of-fold errors by every group that matters to the people using the model, and attach intervals before declaring a failure.
  • Turn the evidence into a short table with a recommendation and a monitoring note.

#Extend it

  • Add a third candidate: logistic regression with a distance_km × item_type interaction (for example with PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True) on one-hot columns). Does it close the laptop gap?
  • Repeat the slice report with Brier score instead of ROC AUC. Which slices are worst calibrated?
  • Simulate the library lending twice as many laptops (resample the test set) and recompute the overall AUC of both models.
  • Turn the reminder rule into a cost: a late return costs 3, a reminder costs 1. Tune a threshold for each model with TunedThresholdClassifierCV and compare costs.

  • scikit-learn: partial_dependence reference (opens in a new tab): the method and response_method options used in Step 4.
  • Google: Model Cards (opens in a new tab): what a short, honest model report covers, including evaluation broken down by subgroup.

What you'll learn

  • Compute a Brier score and a reliability table by hand, and check them against scikit-learn.
  • Choose between sigmoid and isotonic calibration based on how much calibration data you have.
  • Explain why permutation importance must be computed on held-out data.
  • Use ICE curves to expose an interaction that a flat partial dependence curve hides.
  • Recognize the multiple-comparisons trap in slice analysis.
  • Correct the probabilities of a class-weighted model with a prior shift.

Each exercise isolates one idea from the Notes in a small, controlled setting, so you can see the effect clearly before you meet it inside a messy project. Try each one before opening the solution.

#Warm-up: a Brier score in your head

Four predictions and what happened:

Prediction 0.9 0.2 0.6 0.1
Outcome 1 0 0 0

Compute the Brier score by hand, then check with code. Which single prediction costs the most?

Show solution

((0.9 − 1)² + (0.2 − 0)² + (0.6 − 0)² + (0.1 − 0)²) / 4 = (0.01 + 0.04 + 0.36 + 0.01) / 4 = 0.105. The confident-ish 0.6 on a negative contributes 0.36, more than the other three combined.

#Exercise 1: A reliability table by hand

Get out-of-fold GaussianNB probabilities on make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=20, n_informative=4, n_redundant=6, random_state=42). Split them into 5 equal-width bins (0 to 0.2, 0.2 to 0.4, and so on), and for each bin print the number of rows, the mean predicted probability, and the actual share of positives. Then confirm the last two columns with calibration_curve(y, proba, n_bins=5).

Need a hint?

np.digitize(proba, [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]) gives each row a bin number from 0 to 4. Group a DataFrame by that number. calibration_curve returns (prob_true, prob_pred), in that order.

Show solution

Notice the row counts: naive Bayes puts most rows in the two extreme bins, and those bins are badly off. Rows it gives about a 6% chance are positive 24% of the time. A reliability diagram without counts hides how many rows each point represents. strategy="quantile" in calibration_curve makes bins of equal size instead.

#Exercise 2: How much data does isotonic calibration need?

Train a LinearSVC on 2,000 rows of make_classification(n_samples=8000, n_features=20, n_informative=5, random_state=7). Keep 3,000 rows as a calibration pool and the rest as a test set. Wrap the trained SVC in FrozenEstimator and calibrate it with CalibratedClassifierCV using 60, 300, and 3,000 calibration rows, with both method="sigmoid" and method="isotonic". Average the test Brier score over 5 random draws of each size.

Need a hint?

CalibratedClassifierCV(FrozenEstimator(svc), method="isotonic").fit(X_cal, y_cal) uses all the rows you pass for calibration and never refits the SVC. Draw the subsets with rng.choice(len(y_cal), n, replace=False).

Show solution

With 60 rows, isotonic is clearly worse: its staircase follows the noise in a tiny sample. By 300 rows the two are close, and with 3,000 isotonic edges ahead because it can bend in ways a sigmoid can't. Rule of thumb: sigmoid for a few hundred rows, isotonic when you have thousands.

#Exercise 3: Permutation importance on the wrong rows

A forest is trained on make_classification(n_samples=600, n_features=6, n_informative=3, n_redundant=0, flip_y=0.3, shuffle=False, random_state=0), so features 3 to 5 are pure noise and 30% of the labels are flipped at random. Compute permutation importance (accuracy) once on the training rows and once on a 30% test split. Which noise features look useful, and on which set?

Need a hint?

shuffle=False puts the informative features first. Fit RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0) and call permutation_importance twice with scoring="accuracy", changing only the data.

Show solution

On the training rows, shuffling a noise feature costs 3 to 6 points of accuracy, because the forest used those columns to memorize the flipped labels, and shuffling breaks that memory. On test rows the same features are worth about zero, or slightly less. Even the real features look inflated on training rows. Training-set importance measures what the model memorized; test-set importance measures what generalizes.

#Exercise 4: The interaction a flat line hides

Generate X uniform on [−1, 1] with three columns and y = 3 * x0 * sign(x1) + x2 + noise. Fit a RandomForestRegressor, then plot partial dependence and ICE curves for x0. Describe what the average says and what the individual lines say.

Need a hint?

PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(model, X, [0], kind="both", subsample=60) draws both. Color doesn't matter; the shapes do.

Show solution

The thick partial dependence line is almost flat, which on its own would say "x0 doesn't matter". The ICE lines say the opposite: x0 matters a lot, pushing predictions up for rows where x1 is positive and down where it is negative. Whenever ICE lines cross or fan out, look for the feature they depend on.

#Exercise 5: The worst slice always looks bad

Take out-of-fold predictions from a logistic regression on make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=10, flip_y=0.1, random_state=2). Assign every row to one of 20 random groups, which by construction mean nothing, and record the worst group's error rate. Repeat with 200 different random groupings. How much worse than the overall error does the worst random group look, on average?

Need a hint?

groups = np.random.default_rng(trial).integers(0, 20, len(y)). For each grouping, compute max(err[groups == k].mean() for k in range(20)).

Show solution

The overall error is about 18%, yet the worst of 20 meaningless slices sits around 24%. If you slice by 20 features and report the worst, a gap of this size is what you'd see even if the model treated every group identically. Before calling a slice a failure, compare its gap with this kind of random-slice baseline, or check that its bootstrap interval excludes the overall rate.

#Exercise 6: Undo class weighting in one line

Fit LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced") on make_classification(n_samples=6000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.9], random_state=3) (stratified 60/40 split). Its probabilities are inflated. Fix them two ways: by subtracting log(n_negative / n_positive) from its decision_function before applying the sigmoid, and with CalibratedClassifierCV. Compare test Brier scores and mean predicted probability with a plain, unweighted model.

Need a hint?

Balanced weights multiply the positives' weight by n0 / n1, which for logistic regression mostly adds log(n0 / n1) to the intercept. Subtract it back: p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(model.decision_function(X_test) - np.log(n0 / n1)))).

Show solution

The raw weighted model predicts a 34% average where the truth is 10%, and its Brier score is twice the others'. Subtracting the log ratio fixes most of it in one line, because for logistic regression the weighting mostly moved the intercept. CalibratedClassifierCV does slightly better because it learns the correction from data, and both end up close to a model that was never weighted. If you only weighted classes to raise recall at 0.5, the plain model plus a tuned threshold gets you there with no repair needed.

#Challenge: A one-call model card

Write model_card(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, slice_col) that fits the model and prints: test ROC AUC and Brier score, the top three features by test-set permutation importance, and for each value of slice_col the row count, ROC AUC, and a 90% bootstrap interval, marking any slice whose interval lies entirely below the overall AUC. Try it on load_diabetes(as_frame=True, scaled=False) with "progression above 200" as the positive class, a scaled logistic regression as the model, and age bands (under 40, 40 to 54, 55 and over) as the slices.

Need a hint?

Add the slice column to X_test only for grouping; drop it before predicting if it isn't a model feature. Resample row positions with rng.integers(0, n, n) and skip resamples that contain only one class.

Show solution

On this split no age band is flagged: the intervals are wide (a few dozen patients per band) and every one of them contains the overall AUC. That is a useful result, not a boring one. It says the data can't show an age-related weakness, which is different from showing there is none, and a model card should say exactly that.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why a single train/test split can't settle which of two models is better.
  • Choose a capstone project and define its decision, positive class, and slices.
  • Write a plan that fixes the metric, cross-validation scheme, tuning budget, and decision rule before looking at results.
  • Estimate how many model fits the plan needs and how long they will take.

Here is a comparison that could end up in a real report. On the diabetes data, with "progression above 200" as the positive class, a logistic regression and a boosted model are each trained on 75% of the patients and scored with average precision on the other 25%. That one split is repeated with 30 different random seeds.

Logistic regression wins most of the time, by anything from almost nothing to 0.12. On three of the splits, boosting wins. If your project happened to use one of those three seeds, your report would have recommended the wrong model, and nothing in that report would have told you so. The capstone is about making comparisons that can't be fooled this easily.

#The brief

You will deliver a reproducible model-comparison report: a Colab notebook that runs top to bottom with fixed seeds, plus a one-to-two-page write-up. Together they must show:

  1. A decision and a metric. Who uses the model, what they do with its output, and which metric matches that use.
  2. Honest validation. A sealed test set opened once, repeated cross-validation on the rest, and group or time splits where the data needs them.
  3. Bounded tuning. At most three candidate model families plus a baseline, each with a fixed tuning budget, tuned inside the cross-validation.
  4. Imbalance handling. A justified choice between plain training, class weights, and threshold tuning.
  5. Leakage checks. A shuffled-label test, a single-feature scan, and a duplicate or group check.
  6. Calibration. A reliability diagram and Brier score for the finalists, and recalibration if the probabilities will be used.
  7. Interpretation. Permutation importance and at least one partial dependence or ICE plot, with a sentence on what they mean.
  8. Error analysis. Errors by at least two slices, with intervals and a per-slice baseline.
  9. A recommendation and its limits. Which model, at which threshold, with what uncertainty, and what the evidence can't tell you.

#Pick a project

All five can be done in Colab for free. Each later milestone works the same way for all of them; only the data loading and the slices change.

Project Data Positive class and decision Slices to analyse Difficulty
Rare-digit detector load_digits, keep 80 of the 8s (Module 5) an 8; flag images for a human checker the true digit of each false alarm starter
Fast diabetes progression load_diabetes(scaled=False) progression above 200; schedule an earlier follow-up sex, age band, BMI band medium (the starter notebook uses this one)
Late library returns the generated loans table (Module 7) a late return; send a reminder item type, borrower type medium
Customer cancellations the generated export with planted leaks (Module 6) cancels by quarter end; offer a discount plan, contract, region hard: you must find and handle the leaks yourself
Your own dataset a public CSV you download in Colab (UCI, a government open-data portal) your choice, written down first at least two you justify hardest: you also document how the data was collected

Pick the medium projects if this is your first full comparison. Small data like the diabetes set (442 patients) is a feature here, not a bug: it makes uncertainty impossible to ignore.

#Write the plan before you look

Every choice you make after seeing results is a chance to fool yourself: switching to the metric your favourite model wins on, dropping the fold that went badly, tuning "just a bit more". The fix is old and simple. Write the plan first, commit it to the top of your notebook, and treat any later change as something you must report.

Copy this template into a text cell and fill it in:

The last field matters most. A decision rule written in advance stops you from calling a 0.004 gap a win.

#How you'll decide between two models

Repeated cross-validation gives each candidate a score on the same folds, so you compare them fold by fold. A natural idea is a paired t-test on those differences, but it is too confident: the folds share most of their training rows, so their scores are correlated and the test treats them as more independent than they are. Nadeau and Bengio's corrected resampled t-test inflates the variance by a term that depends on the share of data in each test fold. You will implement it in six lines in the next lesson. The video explains why the usual tests break here and which ones are used instead.

#Budget your compute

A plan should fit in your time. Count the fits: each outer fold runs every candidate's search, and each search fits every configuration on every inner fold, plus one refit.

About 270 fits is comfortable on a dataset this size. If your own dataset has 100,000 rows, the same plan might take an hour; shrink the grid, use fewer repeats, or switch to HalvingRandomSearchCV from Module 4 before you start, not halfway through.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Why must the decision rule be written before you see any cross-validation results?

  • It's a rule for you, not for the library.

  • Fixing the rule in advance turns "I think it's better" into a test the result can actually fail.

  • The test set is opened once at the end and never informs the rule.

Show answer

B. Fixing the rule in advance turns "I think it's better" into a test the result can actually fail.

2Your plan has 3 candidates, each with a 6-configuration grid, 3 inner folds, and 5 × 3 outer folds. Roughly how many fits is that?

  • That counts outer folds times configurations but forgets the inner folds and refits.

  • Each candidate needs 15 × (6 × 3 + 1) = 285 fits, and three candidates make 855.

  • That's one candidate's inner search for a single outer fold, without the refit.

Show answer

B. Each candidate needs 15 × (6 × 3 + 1) = 285 fits, and three candidates make 855.

Key takeaways

  • A single split can crown the wrong model; repeated, paired cross-validation is the minimum for a comparison.
  • Write the decision, metric, validation scheme, budget, and decision rule before training anything.
  • Count your fits and time one of them before committing to a plan.
  • Use a corrected test for paired fold scores; plain paired t-tests are overconfident when training sets overlap.

  • Nadeau and Bengio (2003), Inference for the Generalization Error (opens in a new tab): the original paper behind the variance correction.

From here until Milestone 9, X_test and y_test are never used. If you search the notebook for X_test before submitting, it should appear only here and in Milestone 9.

#Milestone 2: Shared folds and a baseline

One outer splitter (5 folds, repeated twice with different shuffles) is shared by every candidate, so fold i means the same rows for all of them. A helper records each candidate's per-fold scores.

The baseline's AP equals the positive share (about 0.27), and its Brier score is what you get by predicting that share for everyone. Every real model must clear both.

#Milestone 3: Tune each candidate inside the folds

Each candidate is a GridSearchCV with a small, fixed grid: that is the bounded budget from the plan. Passing the search object itself to cross_validate makes it nested: on every outer fold, the grid search runs its own 3-fold search on the outer training part only, so the outer score never sees the rows that chose the settings.

Both clear the baseline by a wide margin. Logistic regression is ahead on all three metrics, but the spreads are large. Whether the lead is real is the next milestone's job.

#Milestone 4: A paired comparison and the decision rule

The corrected resampled t-test from the brief works on the per-fold differences. Its only change from an ordinary paired t-test is the extra test_share / (1 - test_share) term, which widens the standard error because overlapping training sets make the folds' scores correlated.

Logistic regression wins 7 of 10 folds by about 0.03 on average, but the corrected test can't rule out chance (p around 0.4). The plan anticipated this: when neither model is clearly better, prefer the simpler, cheaper, easier-to-explain one. That sentence, written before you saw any numbers, is what makes this a decision rather than a preference.

📝 Note

A naive paired t-test on the same ten differences, stats.ttest_rel(a, b), reports p of about 0.16, less than half the corrected value. That difference is the overconfidence the correction removes. With more folds or a slightly bigger gap, the naive test would cross 0.05 while the corrected one would not.

#Milestone 5: Imbalance and the threshold

About 27% of patients are positive, so imbalance is moderate. The plan says to test class weights by AP and to pick the threshold from costs. First, fix the logistic model's C by refitting its search on all development rows.

Class weights change AP by less than 0.01, so we keep the unweighted model and its honest probabilities. The tuned threshold (evaluated with the threshold chosen inside each outer fold, so the comparison is fair) lowers the cost a little and ends up near 0.2, close to the textbook 1 / (1 + 3) = 0.25 for these costs.

#Milestone 6: Check calibration

The threshold logic assumes the probabilities are roughly right, so check them on out-of-fold predictions.

With only about 66 patients per bin the points wobble, but none sits far from the diagonal, and the Brier score is well below the baseline's. No recalibration needed. Write that sentence, with the numbers, into the report.

#Milestone 7: Leak checks

Three quick checks from Module 6. Shuffled labels should drop AP to about the positive share. No single column should be suspiciously strong. Development and test rows must not overlap or repeat.

Shuffled labels give an AP close to the positive share (the small excess is noise from only 331 rows), so the pipeline can't find signal where there is none. The strongest single columns (s5 and bmi, around 0.8 each) are plausible clinical measurements taken at baseline, not consequences of the outcome. There are no duplicates. The diabetes data has one row per patient, so no group split is needed; say so explicitly in the report.

#Milestone 8: Explain the model and slice its errors

Permutation importance uses a held-out slice of the development rows. Slices use the out-of-fold probabilities from Milestone 6, cut at the chosen threshold, with bootstrap intervals.

The miss rate (the share of fast progressors the model fails to flag) is the slice metric that matches the decision, since a miss is the expensive mistake. Read the intervals before the point estimates: with a few dozen fast progressors per slice, every interval is wide and they overlap, so the honest finding is "no slice is detectably worse", plus the sample sizes that limit that claim. The youngest group's miss rate is about twice the middle group's; that is worth listing as something to monitor, not as a finding.

#Milestone 9: Open the test set once, and draft the report

Everything is fixed: model, C, threshold. Fit on all development rows, score the sealed test set once, and let the code write the numbers into the report draft.

The test numbers should land inside the range the cross-validation predicted. If they had been far outside it, the right response would be to report that and investigate, not to go back and change the model, because the test set has now been used.

  • Nest tuning inside the outer folds, share the folds across candidates, and compare with a corrected paired test.

What you'll learn

  • Write unit tests that guard the evaluation itself: sealed test rows, pipelines, seeds, shuffled labels, and a calibration floor.
  • Rewrite metric-heavy sentences as counts and decisions that a non-specialist can act on.
  • Plan a short presentation that leads with the recommendation and shows the uncertainty.
  • Grade your report against the rubric and reflect on the choices you made.

Before anyone trusts your recommendation, a careful reviewer will ask some version of five questions. Did the test set stay sealed? Would the numbers come out the same if I ran it? Could the pipeline find signal in random labels? Are the probabilities usable? Is preprocessing inside the cross-validation? You've answered all of these once, by hand, in the build. This lesson turns the answers into tests that rerun every time you change the notebook, then turns the results into something a person can act on.

#Test the evaluation, not just the model

Unit tests are usually written for application code, but evaluation code breaks too: someone moves the scaler out of the pipeline to "speed things up", or a refactor quietly reuses the test rows. Each test below encodes one of the reviewer's questions. They use the starter project's data and settings; swap in your own loading and model functions.

All five pass. To see one earn its keep, break something on purpose: change make_model to return a bare LogisticRegression and rerun. The pipeline test fails immediately, before a scaler fitted on all the rows can quietly leak into your scores. A test that has never failed for you is a test you can't be sure works, so break each one once.

💡 Tip

In Colab, keep the tests in the last cell of the notebook and run Runtime › Restart session and run all before you submit. A notebook that only works when cells are run in a lucky order isn't reproducible.

#Turn metrics into sentences people can act on

The person deciding whether to use the model probably doesn't think in average precision. They think in patients, follow-up appointments, and missed cases. Your report should translate.

Weak Strong
"The model achieved an AP of 0.758." "Of every 2 patients the model flags, about 1 really is a fast progressor."
"Recall at the tuned threshold is 0.9." "It misses about 1 in 10 fast progressors."
"Logistic regression outperformed boosting." "The two models were within noise of each other; we chose the simpler one, as planned."
"The model is well calibrated." "When it says 30%, about 30% of those patients turn out to be fast progressors."
"No significant subgroup differences." "We couldn't detect a difference between groups, but with only about 25 to 45 fast progressors per group, a real gap of 10 points could have been missed."

A small function keeps these sentences tied to the confusion matrix, so they update whenever the numbers do. These are the test-set counts from the build's final milestone.

The last line is often the one a manager remembers: for each real case found, the clinic books about two appointments. That is the trade the threshold encodes, stated in the clinic's own currency.

#Present it in five slides

A comparison presentation has one job: help the audience make the decision. Lead with the answer, and show uncertainty instead of hiding it.

Slide Title as a full sentence What's on it
1 "We recommend the logistic model at a 21% threshold." The decision, the recommendation, and the plain-words trade from above
2 "We tested on patients the model never saw." The validation diagram: sealed test set, repeated folds, nested tuning
3 "Boosting was not clearly better, so we kept the simpler model." The paired fold-difference chart from Milestone 4
4 "We checked for leaks, bad probabilities, and weak subgroups." Shuffled-label result, reliability diagram, slice table with intervals
5 "What this can't tell you yet." Limitations and what you'd monitor after launch

Notice that every title is a claim, not a topic. "Calibration" tells the audience what the slide is about; "The probabilities can be used as they are" tells them what to conclude.

#The rubric

Grade your own report before you hand it in. Each row is worth up to 3 points.

Criterion 3: excellent 2: solid 1: needs work
Plan and decision Plan written first, with metric, costs, and decision rule; any changes reported Plan present but partly written after results No plan, or metric chosen after seeing scores
Validation Sealed test opened once; repeated CV; group/time split where needed and justified CV and a test set, but one gap (no repeats, or no group check) Single split, or test set used for choices
Tuning budget Nested, bounded search for each candidate; budget counted in advance Tuned on CV but not nested; optimism acknowledged Unbounded or test-set tuning
Imbalance and threshold Weights vs threshold compared with evidence; threshold from costs, chosen inside CV Reasonable choice with partial evidence Default 0.5 with no discussion
Leakage checks Shuffled labels, single-feature scan, duplicates/groups, all reported Two of the three None
Calibration Reliability diagram and Brier for finalists; recalibrated when needed One of the two Probabilities used without checking
Interpretation Permutation importance on held-out data and PDP/ICE, with honest caveats One method, correctly computed Impurity importances read as truth
Error analysis Two or more slices, intervals, per-slice baseline, cautious conclusions Slices without intervals or baseline No slices
Recommendation and limits Clear recommendation in plain words; uncertainty and limits specific to this data Recommendation with generic limits No clear recommendation
Reproducibility Restart-and-run-all works; seeds fixed; tests pass Runs, but needs manual steps Doesn't run top to bottom

27 to 30 is a report you could hand to a real team. Below 20 usually means one of the early rows (plan, validation, leakage) went wrong, and everything downstream inherited it.

#Reflect

Write a short paragraph for each of these at the end of your report. They are graded for honesty, not for having the "right" answer.

  1. Which decision in your plan would you change if you started again, and what result taught you that?
  2. Where did you feel tempted to change a choice after seeing results? What did you do?
  3. Which check (leakage, calibration, slices) changed your mind about something, if any?
  4. What would you need, in data or time, to make your weakest conclusion stronger?
  5. If this model were used for a year, what would you monitor, and what change would make you retrain it?

#Keep going

You now have the habits that separate a model comparison from a leaderboard screenshot. Some directions from here:

  • Fairness and subgroup metrics. Fairlearn (opens in a new tab) turns your slice tables into a MetricFrame with many metrics per group, and adds tools for comparing and mitigating disparities.
  • Interpretation in depth. Christoph Molnar's Interpretable Machine Learning (opens in a new tab) covers SHAP values, accumulated local effects (a fix for partial dependence with correlated features), and more.
  • Models in production. Chip Huyen's books page (opens in a new tab) introduces Designing Machine Learning Systems, which picks up where this course stops: data drift, monitoring, and retraining.
  • Visual explainers. MLU-Explain (opens in a new tab) has interactive articles on ROC curves, precision and recall, bias and variance, and cross-validation that make good refreshers.
  • Practice on harder data. Take the capstone notebook to a public dataset with real mess: missing values, dates, and repeat entities. Competitions are good practice too, as long as you remember that a public leaderboard is a test set that has been peeked at thousands of times.
